On these facts, the limited exclusion order is within the Commission's discretion as reasonably related to stopping the unlawful infringement, and is affirmed.
5820: Trade secret misappropriation: glass packaging information theory; no substantial evidence of misappropriation because Intersil already possessed the information
We therefore conclude that no substantial evidence supports finding misappropriation based on the asserted glass packaging trade secret.
5821: Trade secret misappropriation: photodiode array structure; liability affirmed, though limited to that trade secret
we affirm the verdict of Intersil's liability for trade secret misappropriation, limited to Intersil's use of the photodiode array structure.
5822: Trade secret misappropriation: Build vs. Buy theory; use of financial information was contractually permitted and cannot support liability (error held harmless)
liability for trade secret misappropriation cannot properly rest on the 'Build vs. Buy' theory advanced by TAOS.
5823: Monetary relief for trade secret misappropriation: disgorgement and exemplary damages award vacated, with remand for sales-based relief limited to head-start period
For those reasons, we vacate the jury's monetary award for misappropriation of trade secrets.
5845: Whether Commerce could refuse to extend the 90-day withdrawal deadline under 19 C.F.R. § 351.213(d)(1) by applying a 2011 guidance Notice that effectively rewrote the regulation without notice-and-comment rulemaking; the court held the Notice has no legal standing and the regulation's meaning is clear, so no deference applies.

Since the 2011 Notice was intended to effectively rewrite the substantive meaning of the regulation without going through the necessary notice-and-comment rulemaking, it has no legal standing, and thus provides no basis upon which the Secretary could make his decision.
5846: Merits of the Court of International Trade's decision affirmed without identifying a specific substantive issue; the court expressly did not reach whether the CBP demand letters constitute final agency action.

Without reaching the question whether the demand letters at issue here constitute final agency action, the Court finds that appellants have failed to show that, on the merits, the decision by the Court of International Trade was erroneous.
5915: Union representative-bargaining unit member privilege and unfair labor practice claim: Board held that any such privilege belongs to the employee, not the union representative, so Martin could not assert it.
The Board thus committed no error in holding that Mr. Martin could not assert the privilege.
5922: Statutory interpretation of patent term adjustment limits under 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(2)(C)(i) and 37 C.F.R. § 1.704(c)(8), holding USPTO may not reduce PTA for applicant delay during a period when the applicant could take no reasonable efforts to conclude prosecution.

On the basis of the plain language of the statute, we hold that the USPTO may not count as applicant delay a period of time during which there was no action that the applicant could take to conclude prosecution of the patent.
5947: Interpretation of the PSOBA beneficiary provision, 34 U.S.C. § 10281(a)(4)(B), and 28 C.F.R. § 32.13 under Chevron: the life insurance designation controls, and the claimant's totality-of-circumstances test was rejected.

Congress intended for the life insurance policy to determine the proper beneficiary for PSOB benefits, which required the BJA to analyze the beneficiary designation as set out in the insurance policy.
5948: Application of California insurance law (the Pimentel exceptions to strict compliance: waiver by interpleader and every reasonable effort to change the beneficiary) and substantial-evidence review of the BJA's finding that the designation was never validly changed.
Because the BJA reasonably found that the third exception was not met, the BJA was therefore required to adhere strictly to the terms of the life insurance policy.
5998: Patent term adjustment: whether an after-final submission that continued to argue the merits of a final rejection, and was not a compliant reply under 37 C.F.R. 1.704(b), constituted applicant delay under 35 U.S.C. 154(b)(2)(C); the court upheld the PTO's permissible construction under Chevron.

we hold that it is permissible to interpret an after-final submission that merely continues to argue the merits of an examiner's final rejection as a "fai[lure] to engage in reasonable efforts to conclude prosecution" such that such an applicant submission would not stop the accrual of applicant delay under the PTA statute.
6018: Whether employee termination is excluded from CBA coverage as an impermissible subject, so the arbitrator lacked jurisdiction and refusal to comply was not an unfair labor practice (CSRA/Fausto-based argument); court rejected it, following Capitol Police I.
The complete rejection of the Police's CSRA-based jurisdictional contention in Capitol Police I commands its rejection here.
6019: Whether the Chief of Police Termination approval provisions of the TCA (2 U.S.C. § 1907(e)(1)(B)) bar arbitration of employee termination, either as inconsistent with law or as specifically provided for by federal statute under Fort Stewart; court rejected both.

Because the TCA gives the Capitol Police Board only a piece of the subject matter of employee termination, and even that piece—its stated ratification of the actual termination decision made by the Chief of Police—can be avoided by remaining silent in the face of termination ordered by the Chief of Police, it hardly can be said that the TCA meets the test of Fort Stewart.
6021: Whether the Police's failure to provide information requested by the Union for implementing the arbitral award constitutes an unfair labor practice; court upheld the Board's finding that it does.
Like the Board, we conclude that the Police's challenge lacks merit.
6059: Affirmance of Board unpatentability decision for all claims of U.S. Patent 8,656,125 based on arguments rejected in companion case No. 18-1433; the underlying merits (anticipation/obviousness) are not separately analyzed in this nonprecedential order.
For the reasons explained in that decision, we affirm the Board.
6125: Preemption: whether the Veterans Court's apportionment decision impermissibly preempts New York domestic relations law; the court found no conflict and rejected the preemption argument.
We see no similar conflict here.
6132: Negotiability of Proposal 8 (union burden on agency to show unpaid suspension promotes efficiency); management right to discipline under 5 U.S.C. 7106(a)(2)(A) bars the proposal; enforcement denied
That conclusion is contrary to law and must be reversed
6133: Negotiability of Proposal K (off-site electronic time entry); duty to bargain over de minimis change threshold met and appropriate arrangement under 7106(b)(3); enforcement granted
With respect to Proposal K, the Office of Compliance’s petition to enforce the Compliance Board’s decision is granted.
6134: Negotiability of Proposal L (FLSA supervisor verification); not reasonably related to the agency's changes, so no duty to bargain; enforcement denied
With respect to Proposal L, the Office of Compliance’s petition to enforce the Compliance Board’s decision is denied.
6135: Negotiability of Proposal P (time for daily time and attendance duties); procedure under 7106(b)(2) and no interference with work assignment; enforcement granted
With respect to Proposal P, the Office of Compliance’s petition to enforce the Compliance Board’s decision is granted.
6136: Negotiability of Proposal R (extension requests for directive timelines); procedures within duty to bargain; enforcement granted
With respect to Proposal R, the Office of Compliance’s petition to enforce the Compliance Board’s decision is granted.
6137: Negotiability of Proposal S (accommodations for employees unable to use computer programs); duty to bargain found; enforcement granted
With respect to Proposal S, the Office of Compliance’s petition to enforce the Compliance Board’s decision is granted.
6138: Negotiability of Proposal D (outside-employment prohibition wording); no change in conditions of employment; enforcement denied
We agree with the Police that Proposal D is outside its duty to bargain because the proposal does not relate to a change in conditions of employment.
6139: Negotiability of Proposal E (conditional outside-employment prohibition); no change in conditions of employment; enforcement denied
We agree with the Police that Proposal E is outside of its duty to bargain because the proposal does not relate to a change in conditions of employment.
6140: Negotiability of Proposal G (volunteer firefighter and place-of-abode prohibition); changes de minimis; enforcement denied
We agree with the Police that Proposal G is outside its duty to bargain.
6141: Negotiability of Proposal H (deletion of or administrative from leave prohibition); no change in conditions of employment; enforcement denied
We agree with the Police that Proposal H is outside its duty to bargain because the proposal does not relate to a change in conditions of employment.
6142: Negotiability of Proposal F (definition of primary business for alcohol-serving establishments); no interference with management rights; enforcement granted
With respect to Proposal F, the Office of Compliance’s petition to enforce the Compliance Board’s decision is granted.
6143: Negotiability of Proposal I (intranet availability of leave regulations); Compliance Board order set aside and remanded to determine whether directive changes conditions of employment
With respect to Proposal I, we set aside the Compliance Board’s order and remand for further proceedings on this issue.
6207: Whether the statutory definition of "use in commerce" in 15 U.S.C. §1127, which applies to federal registration, limits liability for trademark infringement under §1125(a); the court held it does not apply to infringement.
This definition does not apply to trademark infringement.
6238: Scope of declaratory and injunctive relief: the court found the Claims Court's remedy imprecise and confusing and vacated it, remanding for a narrower declaration and injunction.
We find that the Claims Court judgment is both imprecise and confusing.
6280: Whether mandamus may be used to obtain review of an unappealed computer reimbursement claim; mandamus cannot substitute for the regular appeals process
Mr. Jackson's reimbursement claim for a computer has not been properly appealed, and mandamus cannot be used "as a substitute for the regular appeals process."
6286: Finding that Rembrandt improperly paid fact witnesses (Attic consultants) contingent on litigation outcome, not clearly erroneous, supporting exceptional-case finding under §285.
The district court's decision does not call these very common agreements into question, id., as Rembrandt suggests, and its finding that the witness payments were improper is not clearly erroneous.
6349: Whether 38 U.S.C. § 714 (VA Accountability Act removal authority) can be applied retroactively to misconduct that occurred before its enactment; held impermissibly retroactive, so the removal was vacated.
We ultimately hold that § 714, properly construed, has impermissible retroactive effect, and that Congress did not authorize the statute's retroactive application.
6386: Whether, after the Board's unpatentability ruling was affirmed, the pending infringement and invalidity case had to terminate in CBS's favor under binding precedent; the panel held it was bound by that precedent and affirmed the judgment for CBS.
The panel lacks authority to reconsider the precedent that Personal Audio agrees was adverse and controlling.
6396: Dismissal of the appeal as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) because the appeal raised claims nearly identical to three previously dismissed appeals and the § 411 argument was frivolous.
we conclude that this appeal is frivolous and must be dismissed under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i).
6398: Competitive injury element of false marking (35 U.S.C. 292(b)), false advertising, and state-law unfair competition claims as to the IntraGrill auger chiller; summary judgment for Morris affirmed because no reasonable factfinder could find the required injury.
We agree with the district court's conclusion, which suffices to affirm summary judgment on all the causes of action involving the IntraGrill auger chiller.
6400: Injury requirement for false marking of the COPE tanks under the '489 patent when the products are properly marked with the '173 patent (Sukumar rule); the record lacks evidence that John Bean would have sold a tank absent the '489 marking.

The record lacks evidence that John Bean would have made or sold a decontamination tank had there been no marking of the COPE products with the '489 patent, even though the marking with the '173 patent remained.
6536: Whether the district court gave adequate notice before entering summary judgment of ineligibility sua sponte on claims 7-8, 11, 14-16 and 18 not in the original motion
Under the circumstances, we see no procedural error in granting summary judgment with respect to claims 7–8, 11, 14–16 and 18.
6539: Entitlement to a retroactive promotion for a reinstated whistleblower; the court held a panel cannot overrule the 'clearly establish' precedent and affirmed the denial of promotion.
This panel, however, does not have the authority to grant Mr. MacLean the relief that he desires. A panel cannot simply overrule its precedent.
6585: Cook's cross-appeal that the Board should have found original claims 5, 8, 17, 19 obvious over Sackier and Kirsch, a ground not asserted in the petitions (Sirona); Board did not err in declining to decide unraised grounds.
[w]e see no error in the Board's decision not to decide grounds of unpatentability not raised in the petition[s].
6596: Consideration of the Hrabal article, outside the pleadings, on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without conversion to summary judgment under Rule 12(d) and judicial-notice limits.

The district court erred in considering the Hrabal article for this purpose without converting Defendants' motion to dismiss into one for summary judgment and giving Plaintiffs a reasonable opportunity to present all pertinent material.
6619: Patent term adjustment under 35 U.S.C. 154(b)(1)(B)(i): whether the post-interference period until mailing of the Notice of Allowance counts as RCE time excluded from B Delay, under 37 C.F.R. 1.703(b)(1) and Novartis.

we hold that, where an RCE has previously been filed, the time between termination of an interference and the date of mailing of the Notice of Allowance is time consumed by continued examination of the application requested by the applicant under section 132(b)
6688: Retroactivity: whether 38 U.S.C. § 714 may be applied to misconduct predating its enactment; court held the § 714 action improper because it depends on pre-enactment conduct.

we hold that the § 714 action brought against Mr. Harrington is improper because the only remaining charges against him depend on conduct predating enactment of § 714, which Sayers concluded is impermissible.
6700: Availability of mandamus to challenge the RO's travertine tile decision and contract dispute; denied because alternative remedies (Board appeal or CBCA appeal) exist.
These "alternative means to attain the desired relief" preclude the grant of mandamus.
6705: Whether Deputy OED Director Griffin validly instituted disciplinary proceedings, given the regulation requiring the OED Director's signature; court applied presumption of permissible delegation and upheld the PTO.
It is, however, well established that delegation of duties is presumptively permissible.
6715: Applicable claim construction standard (BRI versus Phillips) after post-briefing terminal disclaimer; court applied BRI and declined to consider the terminal disclaimer, following Thorington and Heyl
Accordingly, in this case we will review the Board's claim construction under the BRI standard.
6793: Whether the BPCIA (42 U.S.C. § 262(l)) preempts, by field and conflict preemption, state law UCL and conversion remedies for a biosimilar applicant's failure to disclose its aBLA under § 262(l)(2)(A); no existing code fits preemption. Held preempted.
We agree with Sandoz that conflict preemption also bars Amgen's state law claims.
6802: Invalidity under 35 U.S.C. § 305 of reexamination-added claims 128-29, 135, 146, 160-61, 165-67 and 171 as impermissibly broadening the original claims.
we also affirm the district court's conclusion that claims 128–29, 135, 146, 160–61, 165–67, and 171 impermissibly broadened the scope of the claims in the '074 patent.
6847: Whether the Board may cancel challenged claims as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112 in an IPR (statutory scope of IPR under 311(b) and 318(a)); court held it may not.
we hold that the Board may not cancel claims for indefiniteness in an IPR proceeding.
6925: Patent term adjustment: whether the examiner's first restriction requirement satisfied the 35 U.S.C. § 132 notice requirement, ending accrual of A Delay under 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(A)(i). No existing code covers PTA calculation.
We agree with the district court and the PTO that under Pfizer, the examiner's first restriction requirement for the '912 patent satisfied the notice requirement of § 132.
6932: Copyright validity (useful article separability under 17 U.S.C. 101 and idea/expression under 102(b)) for the '458 pencil/chalk holder copyright; the court held Lanard does not own a valid copyright, so infringement was not reached.
Because the chalk holder itself is not copyright protectable, Lanard cannot demonstrate that it holds a valid copyright.
6933: Trade dress infringement: the court held no reasonable trier of fact could find the Lanard Chalk Pencil trade dress acquired secondary meaning.
We agree with the district court that, based on the evidence in the record, no reasonable trier of fact could reach the conclusion that the Lanard Chalk Pencil has acquired secondary meaning.
6934: Statutory and common law unfair competition claims, which rose or fell with the infringement claims and were not separately challenged on appeal.

Thus, because we find that the district court correctly granted summary judgment in favor of Appellees on Lanard's other claims, we hold that the court also correctly granted summary judgment on the unfair competition claims.
6950: Whether state tort claim for tortious interference was preempted by federal patent law absent bad-faith assertion of patent; bad-faith exception applied and jury verdict affirmed

Energy presented sufficient evidence to allow a reasonable fact finder to conclude that HOTF, the patent holder, acted in bad faith, and therefore its claim for tortious interference falls within the bad-faith exception to preemption.
6974: Compensatory damages under 5 U.S.C. 1221(g): MSPB's award of $10,000 in WPA compensatory damages supported by substantial evidence; claimant's request for a larger award rejected
Substantial evidence supports the MSPB's compensatory damages award.
6975: Consequential damages under 5 U.S.C. 1221(g) limited to out-of-pocket costs; no recovery for travel-status burden absent proof of out-of-pocket expenses; affirmed
Substantial evidence supports the MSPB's decision that Mr. Hickey is not entitled to consequential damages.
7039: Mandate rule held inapplicable to the URA attorney fee issue, so the Government may raise its fee arguments again on remand in the Court of Federal Claims.
the mandate rule is inapplicable, and the Government may subsequently raise its arguments with respect to this issue before the Court of Federal Claims.
7053: Whether Commerce had inherent authority to rescind the administrative review of Harmoni as illegitimate ab initio after finding the requesting party's misrepresentations tainted its review request
we are not persuaded that Commerce exceeded its authority when it decided to rescind NMGGC's review of Harmoni as 'illegitimate ab initio.'
7087: Breach of contract claim: summary judgment for Fleet affirmed because the only contracts in the record are between Fleet and Mudguard, not Surti, so no contract with Surti was shown.
Because Mr. Surti has failed to present evidence of a contract between him and Fleet, an essential element of his claim, summary judgment was appropriate.
7088: Misappropriation of trade secrets: summary judgment for Fleet affirmed because the only specifically identified information was disclosed in a published patent application, which is not reasonably maintained as secret.
Placing that information in a patent application is a failure to use such reasonable efforts.
7115: Whether a prior-art analysis can be conducted for means-plus-function claims 7-9 lacking corresponding structure; Board could not reach merits, so unpatentability not shown
In this circumstance, the Board’s necessary course of action was to conclude that unpatentability of claims 7–9 could not be shown.
7145: Whether McCord had to exhaust TRICARE administrative procedures before seeking damages for improper exclusion from TRICARE coverage; the court held exhaustion was not required.
Exhaustion of TRICARE procedures is not required for McCord's claim.
7150: Whether the Veterans Court could grant equitable relief to set an earlier effective date; court held no legal error in declining to exercise equitable powers.
we cannot say that the Veterans Court committed legal error by not exercising its equitable powers to find an effective date earlier than April 2, 2007.
7177: Denial of in forma pauperis status under the PRLA three-strikes rule, 28 U.S.C. §1915(g), including whether the imminent-danger-of-serious-physical-injury exception applied to the Tucker Act complaint; the court found no abuse of discretion in denying IFP status.
The Court of Federal Claims did not abuse its discretion when it held that the three-strikes rule was met by Mr. Fourstar's litigation history.
7199: Denial of injunctive relief in a bid protest after the Claims Court found statutory violations: the court weighed the public interest in veterans' medical supply and the limited remaining contract term, and affirmed denial for the terms expiring April 2020 while remanding for the challenge to be held in abeyance in case of a contract extension.
We conclude that the Claims Court did not abuse its discretion in view of the public interest factor and the limited period remaining on the contracts.
7202: Copyright fair use defense (17 U.S.C. § 107): the court held Google's verbatim copying of the declaring code and SSO of 37 Java API packages was not fair use as a matter of law, reversing the denial of JMOL and remanding for a damages trial. No listed code covers copyright fair use.
we conclude that Google's use of the 37 Java API packages was not fair as a matter of law.
7297: Whether removal was barred as a second adverse action for the same misconduct after a last-chance agreement suspension (bar on successive discipline); court found the disciplines rested on different misconduct.
the act of driving drunk is separate and distinct from the act of being unable to report for duty.
7298: Interpretation and enforcement of the last-chance settlement agreement, including whether the agency had to keep employing or transfer the employee; court held the agency was not so obligated.
the DODEA was "not obligated under the settlement agreement to continue to employ the appellant or to transfer him" regardless of future misconduct.
7363: Correction of the final judgment, which improperly purported to rule on the validity and infringement of unasserted claims; remanded for clerical correction.
Therefore, we remand to allow the district court to correct this clerical error.
7509: Whether an intent-to-use application was void ab initio because the applicant, a co-owner of the YOGI mark, lacked bona fide intent to use it solely in her individual capacity and failed to obtain the consent of all interested parties (15 U.S.C. § 1051(b)).
we find no error in its conclusion that Ms. Puri's application was void ab initio for failing to include or obtain the consent of all interested parties.
7568: Whether the federal conflict-of-interest statutes (18 U.S.C. 203 and 205) apply to a former federal employee's representation of private clients before the PTO; court held they apply and rejected the statutory-scope argument
We therefore reject Mr. Correll's contention that the federal conflict-of-interest statutes do not apply to his conduct.
7597: Copyrightability of nonliteral elements of SAS System and SAS Language software under the abstraction-filtration-comparison test, and burden allocation on protectability after a registration is shown; the court held SAS failed to establish copyrightable elements and affirmed dismissal.

We hold that where the court has received persuasive evidence that the asserted elements are copyright unprotectable, SAS, as the copyright holder, was obligated to identify with specificity the elements of the SAS program that it asserts as copied and to establish that those elements fall within the scope of protection extended to such elements under copyright law.
7613: Personal jurisdiction over foreign defendant Siemens AG: no general jurisdiction and no specific jurisdiction based on the operation of its website; dismissal affirmed.
We also affirm the district court's grant of Siemens AG's motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction.
7639: Sleep Number's commercial-success nexus and 'read on' finding (possible infringement resolution, due process and APA); court declined to reach because the challenge would not change the patentability determination, following SkyHawke.
We decline to address this argument further because American National does not challenge the Board's finding that Sleep Number's evidence of commercial success "has minimal probative weight."
7641: Whether the petition satisfied 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(3) for the means-plus-function term 'pressure sensing means' without an express construction; Board's application of its own rule upheld.
we see no abuse of discretion in the Board's conclusion that American National satisfied the requirements of 37 C.F.R. § 42.104.
7701: Commerce's withdrawal from the 2013 suspension agreement under its contractual section VI.B at-will clause was within its authority and not statutorily improper
we see no reason why Commerce's withdrawal from the suspension agreement pursuant to the agreement's terms exceeded its authority or was otherwise statutorily improper.
7702: Claim that Commerce's 2013 termination was based on improper political influence is foreclosed by Department of Commerce v. New York and fails
the Supreme Court's decision in Department of Commerce v. New York, 139 S. Ct. 2551 (2019), expressly forecloses a challenge based on alleged political influence.
7725: Civil contempt of a consent decree: whether the newly accused product is not more than colorably different and infringes the decreed patents, under the TiVo contempt standard and clear-and-convincing burden; contempt denied.
We conclude that the district court did not abuse its discretion, in that it did not clearly err, in finding insufficient proof of literal infringement.
7794: Interpretation of the statutory term 'producer' in 19 U.S.C. §§ 1673a and 1677(9)(C) for AD industry-support calculation at initiation; court held Eurodif controls and affirmed Commerce's 'stake in the industry' definition and use of the sufficient production-related activities test.
In summary, we affirm Commerce's interpretation of the term "producers" as an entity that requires a stake in the domestic industry.
7795: Whether Commerce's determination that fabricators are not producers for industry-support purposes was supported by substantial evidence (AD initiation industry support).
We agree with Cambria and the government that Commerce's determination was supported by substantial evidence.
7812: Patent term adjustment: whether the PTO properly reduced PTA under 35 U.S.C. §154(b)(2)(C)(i) for time consumed by an after-allowance amendment (Supernus argument); court found the PTO's calculation proper on the merits.
We agree with the PTO on the merits, and we therefore do not reach the issue of forfeiture.
7813: Patent term adjustment: whether 37 C.F.R. §1.704(c)(10) (2019) validly treats an applicant's after-allowance amendment as applicant delay under §154(b)(2)(C)(iii); court applied Chevron step two and upheld the PTO's interpretation.
We therefore find that the PTO's interpretation of the statute was permissible here.
7844: Whether mandamus relief was available to compel the RO to reinstate a claim and issue a Supplemental Statement of the Case where the claimant had not exhausted VA administrative remedies; the court held the first mandamus condition (no other adequate means of relief) was unmet because the ordinary appeal process was not completed.
A writ of mandamus cannot be used by a party to avoid the ordinary appeal process.
7897: Likelihood of success on trade secret misappropriation claim: plaintiff failed to identify its trade secrets, and the asserted secret was publicly disclosed in the patent
As Well Cell cannot describe its alleged trade secrets, it cannot show a likelihood of success on its misappropriation claim.
7942: Mandamus standard: whether the veteran had no other adequate avenue for relief (must file a NOD to obtain Board review and an estimate), so mandamus was improper; affirmed as no abuse of discretion.
The Veterans Court's finding of an adequate alternative avenue of relief is neither an abuse of discretion nor a legal error.
7954: Request to recall the appellate mandate in the prior PTO patent-rejection appeal (In re Hartman) to overturn that decision was denied for lack of extraordinary circumstances.
Ms. Hartman has supplied no legitimate basis for the court to take this extraordinary step.
7964: Whether a related USERRA complaint excused Oram from exhausting the VEOA complaint process with the Department of Labor before going to the Board.
Mr. Oram cites no legal authority for negating the specific terms of the VEOA statute, and we know of none.
7979: Whether the ITC may rescind or modify a civil penalty order under 19 C.F.R. § 210.76 after the asserted patent claims were held invalid, and whether ITC practice in the Magnets and other cases compels modification; court held no abuse of discretion in declining to modify.
We hold that the ITC did not abuse its discretion in declining to rescind or modify its civil penalty order in view of the asserted claims' invalidation.
7986: Whether ex parte reexamination of the '513 patent was properly ordered because the requested questions of patentability were 'new' under 35 U.S.C. § 303(a) (substantial new question of patentability).
Thus, we hold the ex parte reexamination in this case was based on substantial new questions of patentability.
7987: Whether the PTO's discretionary decisions under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) are reviewable under the APA, rejecting the government's argument that they are committed to agency discretion by law.
we reject the government's argument that § 325(d) decisions are not reviewable.
7998: Scope of the Court of International Trade's authority on remand: the CIT exceeded its authority by directing Commerce to reverse its particular market situation finding and reach a specific outcome.
because the Court of International Trade lacks authority to reverse Commerce, we vacate the trial court's opinion to the extent that it directs Commerce to reach a certain outcome.
8038: Prejudicial error standard under Shinseki v. Sanders: the Veterans Court held the veteran to too rigid a standard and too heavy a burden to show prejudice, but the error was harmless because the Board correctly interpreted the regulation.
The Veterans Court applied too rigid of a prejudicial error standard and placed too heavy a burden on Mr. Slaughter to show prejudice.
8050: Whether the Veterans Court properly applied the All Writs Act (28 U.S.C. § 1651(a)) together with 38 U.S.C. § 7261(a)(2) to deny a writ of mandamus compelling VA action on pending claims; the court held the AWA applies and affirmed.
Because we read the AWA and § 7261(a)(2) together, we hold that the Veterans Court's interpretation of the AWA was proper.
8147: Denial of mandamus petition for unreasonable delay in Board adjudication of SMC appeal under the TRAC factors; court found no abuse of discretion in the Veterans Court's TRAC analysis
Thus, the Veterans Court did not abuse its discretion with respect to the first two TRAC factors.
8160: Availability of mandamus under the All Writs Act: court held mandamus was unavailable because the petitioner lacked a clear and indisputable right as to deductibles and had other adequate remedies by appeal to the Board and the Veterans Court.
Mandamus was not available in this case because the petitioner did not have a clear and indisputable right with respect to deductibles and had other adequate legal remedies by appeal.
8281: Enforceability of the settlement agreement against the employee, including claims of duress, lack of drafting participation, and failure to understand the terms; court held the agreement valid and enforceable
Thus, we find the Settlement Agreement valid and enforceable.
8293: Whether pure AIA first-inventor-to-file patents may be subjected to an interference under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §135 and AIA §3(n); court held they may not, reversing the Board's cancellation of SNIPR's patents. Coded as other because no interference-specific code exists.
We agree with SNIPR and hold that pure AIA patents may not be part of an interference.
8328: APA challenges to the PTO's Director Review process: unsigned denial orders, lack of explanation, absence of notice-and-comment rulemaking, and undisclosed advisory committee members; all rejected as not warranting vacatur.
In sum, none of the purported APA violations provides any basis for us to reverse or vacate the Board’s decisions.
8392: Mandamus standard applied to the veteran's petition: failure to exhaust administrative remedies (SMC benefits claim) and no unreasonable delay under the TRAC factors (alleged April 2019 CUE motion); the Veterans Court's denial of mandamus was affirmed.
Because Mr. Wright did not exhaust his administrative remedies, the Veterans Court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the petition for a writ of mandamus.
8416: Alleged bias of the administrative judge; the court held the Bieber standard of deep-seated favoritism or antagonism was not met.
Mr. Kolenc has not shown how the AJ's statement is evidence of deep-seated favoritism or antagonism, and thus he has not satisfied the high standard set out in Bieber.
8491: Denial of intervention as of right under CIT Rule 24(a)(2): whether domestic steel producers who objected to Section 232 exclusion requests have a legally protectable interest; the court held they do not.
any scheme such as Commerce's here that effectively permits anyone to participate in administrative proceedings confers a legally protectable interest on no one.
8519: Arbitrator's citation of state law rather than the federal substantive standard; court found the error harmless or extraneous and declined to reverse
However, because the arbitrator's citation of state law was either harmless or extraneous, we decline to reverse his determination.
8528: Rule 12(d) conversion: the district court erred by considering matters outside the pleadings without expressly rejecting them or converting the motion, but the error was held harmless because the dismissal did not hinge on the extraneous material.
But we hold that the district court's error was harmless.
8550: Argument that the Board erred in classifying the disability solely under diagnostic code 7800; court held it legally precluded by the terms of the 2018 settlement stipulation.
That argument is legally precluded by Mr. Bennett's settlement with the government, which provided that the VA would classify his "pseudofolliculitis barbae with disfigurement"
8554: Request that the unreviewed ALJ determinations (obviousness over Meiller, Park and other references) be vacated by operation of law under the Munsingwear equitable tradition; the court declined to vacate.
We do not agree that the ALJ's determinations that the Commission chose to review but on which it took no position should be vacated by operation of law.
8581: Request to remove the Claims Court judge for bias based on the description of plaintiff's claims as 'sly'; court held the standards for removal were not met.
Mr. Straw has not satisfied the standards for removal.
8700: Scope of the ineligibility judgment: vacated insofar as it held unasserted claims (other than claims 1 and 31-33) ineligible, because the operative complaint asserted only those claims.
we conclude that the ineligibility judgment should apply to only claims 1 and 31–33 of the asserted patents.
8753: Mandamus unavailable where an alternative adequate remedy exists: the IMO request can be pursued in the direct appeal before the Board, so denial of the writ to compel an IMO was affirmed.

Because the Board will address the IMO request in the direct appeal, Mr. Proceviat will be afforded an alternative means to pursue relief and is therefore not entitled to a writ compelling the VA to provide him an IMO.
8754: Denial of mandamus on the TRAC unreasonable-delay factors for the IMO request, with the Veterans Court's TRAC analysis affirmed as not showing clear error.
the court considered the TRAC factors and concluded they do not weigh in petitioner's favor.
8767: Mandamus standard under the All Writs Act and TRAC factors for unreasonable delay in VA proceedings; Federal Circuit found no legal error in the Veterans Court's denial of mandamus.
Although Jones is understandably frustrated by the delays in processing his claim, we discern no legal error in the Veterans Court's decision to deny his petition for a writ of mandamus.
8771: Request to remove the Claims Court judge for alleged political bias; request denied as without merit.
As this court found with respect to another of Mr. Straw's appeals raising the same allegations against the same Claims Court judge, this claim has no merit.
8775: Whether the Veterans Court abused its discretion in denying mandamus relief to compel VA processing of CUE claims and use of the AMA review system (mandamus standard and adequate alternative means)
We conclude that the Veterans Court did not abuse its discretion in denying Mr. Haro's petition.
8876: Whether the PTO erred in treating the rehearing request as a request for Director review rather than a Board rehearing; the court assumed error but held it harmless, so no remand was required.
we conclude that the error was harmless.
8904: Whether the ex parte reexamination requests raised a substantial new question of patentability (a factual finding reviewed for substantial evidence), supporting the reexaminations.
We agree with the USPTO that the Board's determination that the reexamination requests raised a substantial new question of patentability was supported by substantial evidence.
8982: Whether the TSS algorithm was a trade secret under the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (generally known / ready ascertainability); no existing code covers trade secret existence.
The district court therefore did not err in finding that Masimo is likely to succeed in showing the TSS to be a trade secret.
9010: Whether Commerce violated 19 U.S.C. §1677m(d) by refusing to notify Hyundai of a deficiency and denying an opportunity to remedy or explain it, and whether Hyundai may supplement the record on service-related revenue.
Commerce erred in denying the opportunity to remedy the asserted deficiency.
9015: Whether Commerce should have rescinded the administrative review under 19 C.F.R. 351.213(d)(3) because no entries were made in the review period; court held rescission not required because Commerce never conclusively found no entries.
Neither the regulation nor Allegheny Ludlum requires rescission of an administrative review where the exporter has failed to establish the absence of entries
9110: Personal jurisdiction and validity of alternative service on a foreign defendant under FRCP 4(f)(3), including whether service violated the Hague Convention, Austrian law, or due process.
the district court did not abuse its discretion in granting alternative service and did not err in denying Mizrahi's motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction.
9122: Whether time spent in appeals to the PTAB that were ended by examiner reopenings of prosecution qualifies for C-delay patent term adjustment under 35 U.S.C. §154(b)(1)(C)(iii) and 37 C.F.R. §§1.702(e), 1.703(e); held that the 'decision in the review reversing' requirement needs a Board or court reversal decision.

That language, we conclude, is reasonably interpreted—indeed, is best interpreted—to require a reversal decision made by the Board or a reviewing court, thus excluding time spent on a path pursuing such a decision when, because of an examiner reopening of prosecution, no such decision is ever issued.
9178: Whether federal law (the ACA, HHS regulations including the Netting Regulation, and the federal scheme) preempts Colorado law fixing creditor priority during insurer insolvency; court held no preemption.
we hold the federal scheme does not preempt Colorado's creditor priority framework.
9181: Scope of the record rule under 38 U.S.C. § 7252(b): the court rejected the Government's argument, raised for the first time on appeal, that constructive possession of documents not before VA adjudicators is contrary to the record rule.
Similarly, the Government argues, for the first time on appeal, that “[t]he constructive possession doctrine is contrary to the clear meaning of 38 U.S.C. § 7252(b)” ... Both are incorrect.
9195: Request to hold the appeal in abeyance pending Supreme Court review of Arthrex Appointments Clause issues, denied.
Given this forfeiture, we decline to hold this case in abeyance pending Supreme Court review of the Appointments Clause issues addressed in that decision.
9236: Reduction of EAJA attorney fees by 60.6 hours for unreasonable sanctions-motion work; dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because it turns on a factual determination reviewable only as a fact challenge under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2).
We are without jurisdiction to review such a factual finding and Robinson fails to articulate any error of law made by the Veterans Court. We, therefore, dismiss this aspect of Robinson's appeal.
9273: Whether the compulsory-counterclaim rule of Fed. R. Civ. P. 13 authorizes entry of a noninfringement judgment in the same action as to patents listed in the declaratory-judgment complaint but not counterclaimed; held that it does not, so the judgment was vacated.
the best understanding of the compulsory-counterclaim rule is that it bars future claims but does not authorize rendering adverse judgment on such claims in the same action
9282: Mandamus standard under Cheney: whether the petitioner lacked other adequate means to obtain the relief (the first Cheney requirement); the Veterans Court's finding that her pending Board appeal was an adequate alternative was affirmed.

Ms. Kramer's February 2020 appeal is her adequate alternative means to attain relief, and thus, Ms. Kramer is unable to satisfy Cheney's first requirement, that she has no other adequate means besides a writ of mandamus to obtain the relief she desires.
9283: Whether the Veterans Court had to apply the TRAC factors to a mandamus petition alleging unreasonable delay where the relief sought was an outcome-specific order; the court held no error because mandamus cannot compel such relief.
A writ of mandamus may not be used to compel an outcome-specific order.
9339: Denial of mandamus relief compelling the Board to decide a delayed VR&E discontinuance appeal, under the TRAC factors; the court found no abuse of discretion in the Veterans Court's denial.
We see no abuse of discretion or legal error in that result.
9351: Whether the arbitrator, rather than the court, must decide arbitrability under the TLA's incorporated CCCP provisions (clear and unmistakable delegation of arbitrability to the arbitrator)
we agree that an arbitrator must determine arbitrability of the dispute between ROHM USA and MaxPower Semiconductor, Inc. ("MaxPower"), we affirm.
9352: Interference priority award: whether the Board properly awarded priority to Agilent based on actual reduction to practice preceding Dionex's earliest alleged conception and sufficient corroboration under the rule of reason, which the court affirmed by incorporating Dionex I.
For those reasons, we affirm the Board's judgment.
9383: Whether the Board exceeded its statutory authority under 35 U.S.C. § 311(b) by deciding written description issues in an IPR limited to §102/103 grounds; court held it did not, under Arthrex.
As in that case, Appellees complied with § 311(b) by asserting invalidity grounds under § 103.
9388: Allocation of burden of proof in an IPR: whether the Board improperly placed on the patent owner the burden to disprove a reasonable expectation of success, where the petitioner bears the ultimate burden.

The fact that the petitioner bears the burden of proof in a Board proceeding does not eliminate the patent owner's burden to proffer opposing evidence against the petitioner's showing of unpatentability.
9455: Whether Customs was required by statute to follow the penalty procedures of 19 U.S.C. §1592(b) before collecting lost duties under §1592(d) when no penalty is assessed; the court held such procedures were not statutorily required.
Thus, when a penalty is not assessed, as here, the statute does not mandate the performance of the procedures under § 1592(b).
9522: Federal dilution by blurring claim under Sections 13 and 43(c): dismissed because P&S failed to prove its INDUSTRY marks or family of marks are famous.

Because P&S does not point to any evidence it presented but that was not adequately considered by the Board, we conclude that the Board's decision with respect to P&S's dilution claim is supported by substantial evidence.
9533: Contract interpretation under New York law: VDG's duty to defend Peloton survived termination of the 2014 agreement and extended to VR Optics' suit over Bike Intellectual Property.
the unambiguous terms of the contract clarify that VDG's duty to defend Peloton survived the termination of the agreement.
9534: Peloton's fraudulent concealment claim against VDG failed at summary judgment for lack of evidence of actual reliance by clear and convincing evidence.
We agree with the district court. Peloton presents only attorney argument that it would have taken action to terminate the agreement or purchase the '513 patent
9535: Peloton's implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing claim against VDG failed because Peloton was not deprived of the benefits of the contract given the invalidity ruling.
Because it has not been deprived of the right to receive its contracted-for benefits, Peloton thus cannot bring a claim for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
9536: Peloton's breach of warranty claim against VDG failed because the patent is invalid and so VDG did not breach its non-infringement warranty.
Because we affirm the district court's invalidity finding, we also affirm the court's granting of summary judgment that VDG did not breach its warranty.
9537: Peloton's tortious interference claim against Coffey and Villency failed because they were not shown to have acted outside the bounds of their authority as VDG employees.
Peloton has produced no evidence that [Mr.] Villency and [Mr.] Coffey were acting outside the bounds of their authority or in their own interest
9546: APA notice-and-comment: whether the USPTO domicile address requirement (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.32(a)(2), 2.189) was a procedural rule excepted from notice-and-comment rulemaking under 5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(A), and whether 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2) overrides that exception
The USPTO's requirement for applicants to provide a domicile address under 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.32(a)(2) and 2.189 is therefore a procedural rule that is excepted from notice-and-comment rulemaking.
9548: Design patent invalidity for functionality (design dictated by function under Sport Dimension factors); no specific code fits, so coded as Other.
We agree with GEM that the district court did not commit clear error when it found the design of the ’828 patent to be functional.
9550: Common law trademark non-infringement (likelihood of confusion under Sleekcraft factors) in a patent declaratory-judgment action; no trademark-specific code applies in a patent case, so coded as Other.
Thus, we affirm the court’s holding that the “TROLLEY BAGS” common law trademark was not infringed.
9557: Validity and enforceability of the settlement agreement and modified settlement agreement despite the unsigned designation of representative form and the question of counsel's authority to settle (5 C.F.R. § 1201.31(a)).
We agree with the Board that petitioner's failure to sign the designation of representative form does not invalidate the settlement agreement or the modified settlement agreement.
9600: Lanham Act false advertising (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B)): the court affirmed JMOL for Next Caller because there was insufficient evidence of materiality (customer reliance or likelihood of influencing purchasing decisions) under Third Circuit law.
Because of the deficiency in proof to establish materiality, we affirm the district court's decision finding no Lanham Act violation under Third Circuit law.
9601: Lanham Act price disgorgement theory under Williamson-Dickie: the court held the disgorgement remedy unavailable because TRUSTID failed to establish the other elements of a false advertising claim, including materiality, so the theory was inapposite.
Because TRUSTID failed in that respect, the price disgorgement theory advanced in Williamson-Dickie is inapposite.
9626: Whether the United States was required to exhaust the city's administrative stormwater appeal process before suing or defending; the court held exhaustion was not required because the appeal process is permissive and solely forward-looking.
The USACE was not required to exhaust the appeal process. As a result, the trial court did not abuse its discretion by refusing to mandate exhaustion.
9679: Mandamus petition alleging unreasonable delay in VA adjudication of an overpayment claim; the court vacated the Veterans Court's denial of mandamus and remanded for reconsideration under the TRAC factors in light of the RO's intervening remand determination.
we vacate the Veterans Court's order denying mandamus and remand to the Veterans Court for reconsideration of the mandamus petition in light of the RO's partial determination.
9692: Federal Vacancies Reform Act challenge: whether the FVRA applies to the Director's delegable rehearing-review function; court held the FVRA reaches only non-delegable duties.
Because the FVRA applies only to non-delegable functions and duties, and because deciding rehearing requests is a delegable duty, we hold that the FVRA does not apply here.
9697: Whether the Board had statutory authority under 35 U.S.C. § 311(b) to decide written description and priority during an IPR; court held the Board could consider it.
Section 311(b), however, merely dictates the grounds on which an IPR petition may be based, not the issues that the Board may consider to resolve those grounds.
9724: Mandamus standard: whether the petitioner had no other adequate means to obtain relief (mandamus prerequisites), so the writ was properly denied on the AMA-participation and CUE-processing claims.

Because he presents no evidence showing that he cannot adequately protect his rights by challenging the RO's March 2019 rating decision through the VA's normal appeals process, Resendez fails to show that the Veterans Court erred in denying his petition for a writ of mandamus.
9758: Trade dress invalidity: summary judgment that Mosaic's trade dress is functional under Lanham Act and Ninth Circuit law, affirmed (trade dress is not a patent or trademark registration code).
we affirm on the ground that the SMCII's design is functional.
9787: Tortious interference counterclaim: whether state-law tort liability is preempted and whether SSI's pre-litigation communications were protected under Noerr-Pennington and objective baselessness (Globetrotter); summary judgment for SSI affirmed.
We affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment to SSI on the tortious interference counterclaim.
9806: Judicial estoppel: whether the district court properly invoked judicial estoppel against AlexSam based on its positions before the PTAB and the district court; the court held the finding that AlexSam took an inconsistent position was clearly erroneous and the estoppel invocation an abuse of discretion.
We agree that AlexSam's arguments have been consistent.
9833: Mandamus denied because an adequate alternative avenue of relief existed (appeal of the Board's eventual decision on remand), so the extraordinary writ was not warranted.
We find that the Veterans Court's finding that an adequate alternate avenue of relief exists is neither legally incorrect nor an abuse of discretion.
9834: Mandamus claim of unreasonable VA/Board delay in implementing the Veterans Court remand order; no unreasonable delay found given the time available and the period the case was pending on appeal.

Under these circumstances, we find no legal error or abuse of discretion in the Veterans Court's finding that Mr. Philippeaux failed to show that VA has unreasonably delaying implementing the remand order.
9872: Burden of proof in ex parte examination: whether the PTO must bear the burden on operability when it challenges claims as contrary to scientific principles; the court held the Board did not err in requiring the applicant to establish operability.
The Board did not err in requiring Hu to establish the operability of his asserted discoveries, in view of the conflict with ordinary experience as well as with established scientific principles.
9895: Dismissal of claims against the Board of Directors of Sorrento Therapeutics on the ground that the board lacks capacity to be sued as a separate entity.
We next agree that Siegler fails to state a cognizable claim against the Board of Directors of Sorrento Therapeutics because it is not a separate legal entity from Sorrento Therapeutics.
9933: Whether the agency complied with an arbitrator's reinstatement order by reinstating the employee to a substantially equivalent position after her former position was abolished (status quo ante compliance/enforcement of reinstatement).

We see no error in the arbitrator's assessment that the two positions are substantially equivalent and commensurate with Ms. Reid's skills and experience, and that appointment to the proposed TSO Economist position would be as close as possible to her prior TBP Economist position.
9949: Weight given to petitioner's expert testimony and expert's qualification as a person of ordinary skill in the art (abuse of discretion review); Board did not abuse discretion and any error was harmless.
The Board did not abuse its discretion.
9956: Validity of the stipulated judgment of non-infringement: the court held the stipulation ambiguous (unclear which claims, constructions and accused products form the basis) and so not reviewable under Jang, requiring vacatur and remand to clarify non-infringement positions.

We must vacate the judgment and remand to the district court for further proceedings to clarify the parties' non-infringement positions, and to determine whether a stipulation of non-infringement is even possible in the circumstances of this case.
10019: Enforceability of mediated settlement agreement (mutual assent and material terms under Texas/federal contract law), enforced by the district court and affirmed
In sum, we affirm the district court's determination that there was a binding settlement agreement between the parties.
10063: Statutory meaning of 35 U.S.C. 154(b)(1)(C)(iii) as applied to the '476 patent: whether a Board affirmance on a new ground of rejection that leaves the claim unpatentable is a reversal of an adverse determination of patentability, so the patent is eligible for Type C PTA. Court held no reversal occurred.
The appeal thus resulted in no substantive change in the patentability of claim 11.
10064: Statutory meaning of 35 U.S.C. 154(b)(1)(C)(iii) as applied to the '476 patent: whether the patent issued under a decision in the review when the claim issued only after substantive post-appeal amendment. Court held it did not.
The statutory requirement is not met if the claim that ultimately issues differs substantively from the claim under review.
10065: Statutory meaning of 35 U.S.C. 154(b)(1)(C)(iii) as applied to the '796 patent: whether an appeal that reversed only the anticipation rejection, while a provisional double patenting rejection remained, reversed an adverse determination of patentability, and whether the patent issued under the decision when the appealed claim was cancelled. Court held neither requirement was met.
The '796 patent therefore did not issue under a decision in the review.
10097: Trade-secret misappropriation and breach of nondisclosure agreement liability: court reversed denial of JMOL because no reasonable jury could find a trade secret or misappropriation.
we conclude that no reasonable jury could have found either trade-secret misappropriation or breach of contract.
10124: Scope of review: the Veterans Court impermissibly engaged in appellate fact finding (whether ear pain is linked to hearing loss and meets Thun) instead of remanding to the Board; court vacated and remanded for Board fact finding.
As an appellate court, the Veterans Court cannot generally render fact findings in the first instance.
10177: Denial of the parties' joint motion to terminate the IPRs under 35 U.S.C. § 317(a) after the Board had already decided the merits; untimely motion and Board discretion to proceed to a final written decision.
Second, the Board correctly identified Polaris's motion as untimely.
10244: Whether a global settlement agreement waiving pending Board appeals bars appeal of Board decisions dismissing the compliance and IRA cases as settled, and whether enforcement of the settlement can be raised in those cases.
Because the parties entered into a lawful settlement agreement freely executed by Ms. Hammond and the Board accordingly dismissed her compliance and IRA cases, she may no longer appeal either case.
10254: Return rights under 10 U.S.C. §1586: the court held the employee did not establish a violation because he retained his position of record and did not satisfactorily complete his overseas duty.
Mr. Chin-Young has not shown that the Agency violated § 1586
10262: Right to rebuttal of the Verification Report under 19 C.F.R. § 165.23(c)(1) as new factual information; court decided on the regulation and did not reach the constitutional rebuttal question.
We need not reach the constitutional question of a right to rebuttal because we conclude that the regulations themselves provide the right to rebut because CBP relied on new factual information.
10281: Federal patent-law preemption of state-law tort claims based on patent-enforcement communications: bad-faith requirement, including whether infringement allegations were objectively baseless; the court held the district court applied incorrect legal principles in finding objective baselessness.
HBL's state-law claims here thus "can survive federal preemption only to the extent that those claims are based on a showing of 'bad faith' action in asserting infringement."
10296: Whether Commerce had statutory authority under the URAA (19 U.S.C. 1677f-1(e), 1677m, 3513(a)) to promulgate the expedited-review regulation, 19 C.F.R. 351.214(k), allowing noninvestigated exporters to obtain individual CVD rates after a CVD order.

We hold otherwise, concluding that the Secretary had statutory authority to adopt the expedited-review process as procedures for implementing statutory provisions that authorize individualized determinations in CVD proceedings.
10349: Whether Pure Hemp was the prevailing party under 35 U.S.C. § 285 after stipulated dismissal with prejudice; the district court erred but the error was harmless
The district court committed error in not finding Pure Hemp to be the prevailing party in this action. However, this error was harmless.
10361: Commerce's cancellation of verification under 19 U.S.C. 1677m(e) on the ground that the submitted information was unverifiable and incomplete was upheld.
Commerce's decision to cancel verification was also supported by substantial evidence and not contrary to law.
10388: Morehouse equitable defense (opposer not damaged by a second registration where an existing registration covers the same mark and services): the Board's striking of the defense was not an abuse of discretion, and the court affirmed.
10399: Whether the interim relief statute, 5 U.S.C. § 7701(b)(2), and the interim relief order barred the agency from initiating and effecting a second removal action while the first removal appeal was pending before the Board.
The interim relief statute does not preclude a second removal action while a first removal action is still pending when the second action cures a procedural deficiency in the first action.
10407: Whether defects in service of the cancellation petition required dismissal; court found the notice function was served and any defect was not prejudicial
We see no error in the Board's service-related analysis finding that the notice function of service was completed, and any defect in service was not prejudicial to Mr. Ghomeshi.
10410: Alleged fraud by StrongVolt in the cancellation proceeding (false certificate of service, officer representations, LexisNexis report) as a basis for reversal; rejected for lack of credible evidence and prejudice

We decline to reverse the Board on this basis because Mr. Ghomeshi fails to present any credible evidence that any of these statements or documents are fraudulent or were made or submitted with deceptive intent.
10423: Scope of the Veterans Court's authority to find facts and weigh evidence in the first instance when entertaining a newly raised argument (38 U.S.C. § 7261), with the court holding the Veterans Court exceeded that authority as to the January 1964 rash location and the weighing of in-service symptom relevance.

We agree with Mr. Stinson that the Veterans Court impermissibly found as a matter of fact, and in the first instance, that Mr. Stinson's January 1964 rash was in a different location than his BPDCN lesion.
10470: The Secretary's delegation of power to deny equitable relief under 38 U.S.C. § 503 to subordinate VR&E Service officials was not shown to be improper.
the Secretary has delegated his power to deny equitable relief to his subordinates
10504: Entitlement to retroactive restoration to a requested position under 5 C.F.R. § 353.301(c); employee removed for cause unrelated to the compensable injury is not entitled to restoration, and the Board's misstatement of the record was harmless.
an employee removed for cause, rather than for reasons substantially related to their compensable injury, is not entitled to restoration.
10526: Alternative holding that the Commission satisfied its statutory duty under 19 U.S.C. 1337(b)(2) to consult with HHS and FDA through Federal Register notice and written solicitation of agency submissions.
Even in the absence of forfeiture, we conclude that, in this case, the Commission satisfied its duty to 'consult with' HHS and the FDA.
10541: Equitable entitlement to Munsingwear vacatur of the Board's February 2019 remand decision finding new reexamination claims 49 and 50 unpatentable, after the '021 patent expired before the decision issued; the majority granted vacatur, rejecting Vicor's argument that SynQor forfeited the equitable right through its own conduct.
Accordingly, we grant SynQor's request for vacatur.
10543: Waiver of contractual right to compel arbitration: whether BESCO substantially invoked the judicial process to Cajun's prejudice, so that it waived arbitration of the contract and non-contract claims (Fifth Circuit law applied to a motion to compel arbitration in a patent-related case)
The district court did not clearly err in finding that BESCO substantially invoked the judicial process with respect to both the contract and non-contract claims.
10592: Bona fide intent to use under Lanham Act section 1(b) in Tiger Lily's opposition to Barclays' application; Board found Barclays had bona fide intent, so the opposition was dismissed.
In this case, we agree with Barclays that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding regarding Barclays' bona fide intent.
10604: New Jersey common-law misappropriation of idea: whether the economic loss doctrine bars the tort claim where a confidentiality agreement governs the idea. Court held the doctrine does not bar the claim.

We conclude that the New Jersey Supreme Court would follow the Restatements and not bar the misappropriation of idea claim under the economic loss rule where there is a confidentiality agreement protecting the idea.
10605: Misappropriation of idea: sufficiency of evidence of use of the idea (Rule 50(b) JMOL denial). Court held there was ample evidence to support liability.
We conclude that there is ample evidence from which a jury reasonably could find liability, and the district did not err in denying judgment as a matter of law on this ground.
10606: Measure of misappropriation damages: whether damages are limited to the head-start period after the idea became public. Court held plaintiffs are limited to head-start damages, reversed denial of new trial and vacated the damages award.
We conclude that, as a matter of law, plaintiffs are limited to head-start damages and did not provide evidence that would support the damages award of over $11 million.
10616: Whether the President can be named as a defendant directly under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i); court held the Trade Court should have dismissed the President because the statute does not authorize proceedings directly against the President.
The Trade Court should have dismissed the President.
10632: Law-of-the-case bar: the Fifth Amendment takings claim, dismissed in a prior appeal and not remanded, could not be re-raised on appeal from the remand.
Dr. Aljindi thus cannot re-raise this issue on appeal from that remand.
10736: Contract interpretation under Delaware law of a mutual confidentiality agreement's forum selection clause, holding it precludes filing IPR petitions during the two-year post-Covenant Term period (breach-of-contract likelihood of success).

We conclude as a matter of law that the forum selection clause in Section 10 of the MCA precludes the filing of IPR petitions during the two-year period following the expiration of the Covenant Term on June 21, 2021.
10752: Judicial disqualification under 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4) based on the trial judge's wife's ownership of Cisco stock; whether placing the stock in a blind trust qualified as divestiture under § 455(f); judge was disqualified from further proceedings
we hold that placing assets in a blind trust is not divestment under § 455(f), and Judge Morgan was disqualified from further proceedings in the case under § 455(b)(4).
10753: Remedy for the § 455(b)(4) violation: whether the post-August 11, 2020 rulings must be vacated under the Liljeberg harmless-error analysis; court held the error was not harmless and vacated the infringement and damages opinion, the post-judgment order, and the recusal denial
Because we find Judge Morgan's violation of § 455(b)(4) was not harmless error, vacatur is the appropriate remedy.
10836: Validity and scoring of Question 5 on the April 2018 Customs Broker License Examination: whether the answer 'E. Foreign Trade Zone Entry' was a correct answer, so that credit should have been given. The court found CBP's denial of credit unsupported by substantial evidence, though it did not change the overall result.

Because the parties agree that the process of admission set forth in [19 C.F.R. § 146.32(a)(1)] does not constitute customs business that is required to be performed by a licensed customs broker, we find that CBP's decision to deny Mr. Chae credit for Question 5 is not supported by substantial evidence.
10837: Validity and scoring of Question 27 on the April 2018 Customs Broker License Examination: whether answer B (packages addressed to U.S. officials containing merchandise) was a correct answer, given 19 C.F.R. §§ 145.2(b), 145.37 and 145.38.
CBP's decision to deny Mr. Chae credit for his answer to Question 27 is supported by substantial evidence, and thus the CIT's decision as to this question is affirmed.
10838: Validity and scoring of Question 33 on the April 2018 Customs Broker License Examination: whether the classification question was ambiguous given the 'current-production' wording, and whether answer B was the best answer under HTSUS Chapter 49 and Chapter 97 Note 2.
We conclude that CBP's decision to deny Mr. Chae credit for his answer to Question 33 is supported by substantial evidence, and thus the CIT's decision as to this question is affirmed.
10840: Availability of the unclean hands defense in Board cancellation proceedings involving functionality; the court held the Board spoke too strongly in suggesting a categorical bar, but the error was harmless because the Board considered the defense case-by-case.
We agree that the Board spoke too strongly by suggesting that the unclean hands defense was categorically unavailable in functionality proceedings.
10902: Whether the Board could render a patentability determination despite Nichia's alleged indefiniteness/logical impossibility in claim 1; the court held the Board may decide patentability because it was not logically impossible to do so.
The Board was also correct in rendering its patentability determination because it was not impossible to do so.
10923: Mandamus requirement of no adequate alternative means: whether a direct appeal under 38 U.S.C. § 502 was an adequate alternative to the writ, held not adequate because the veterans did not challenge a VA rule.
Thus, the Beaudettes had no adequate alternative means to obtain the relief requested and the Veterans Court properly issued a writ of mandamus.
10949: Vacatur of infringement judgment on '948 and '548 patent claims after the PTAB's unpatentability decision was affirmed on appeal (XY, LLC rule that accused infringer need not keep defending adjudged-invalid patent).
Therefore, we vacate the infringement judgment as to those invalid claims.
10990: Discretionary dismissal of claims as frivolous (hacked email account allegations lacking factual support).
We discern no abuse of discretion in the trial court's determination.
11017: Preliminary injunction against Sunset's sale and marketing of filters under the Lanham Act (likelihood of success, presumption of irreparable harm under the Trademark Modernization Act, balance of equities and public interest); the court affirmed the narrowed injunction.
For all of these reasons, we affirm the district court's grant of the preliminary injunction.
11023: Remedy scope for bid protest injunctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(2) and whether a remand was required instead of injunctive relief; court held injunction within discretion.
In sum, the Claims Court has the authority to either issue an injunction or remand to the agency, and determining the appropriate course may depend on the facts at hand.
11025: Judicial estoppel barring petitioner Intel from advancing on appeal a claim construction inconsistent with the construction it advocated before the Board.
Intel is judicially estopped from raising this argument.
11055: Statutory authority under 35 U.S.C. § 3(b)(3) for the Director to delegate rehearing review to the Commissioner for Patents; court rejected the argument that the Patent Act does not authorize such delegation.
Our determination that § 3(b)(3) authorized the delegation to the Commissioner forecloses Fall Line's argument to the contrary.
11071: Morehouse prior-registration defense held inapplicable to bar the challenge to the opposition, because the applied-for mark claims rights in BROOKLYN and the registered mark disclaims them.
The Morehouse defense does not apply.
11093: Whether the agency complied with the January 2011 settlement agreement (retirement contribution payment and reinstatement), as found by the MSPB and reviewed for substantial evidence
We conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's determination that the agency complied with the Settlement.
11094: Scope of MSPB authority to enforce a settlement agreement: whether the Board could award back pay, fees, costs and other benefits outside the settlement for alleged breach
The [Board] does not possess authority to award monetary damages for the breach of a settlement agreement.
11112: Denial of injunctive relief (set aside of size determination, declaration of small business status, reinstatement as awardee) because the protester did not succeed on the merits of its bid protest claim.
There can be no injunctive relief without a corresponding prevailing claim.
11124: Plaintiff's claim that the trial judge was biased (based on the appointing President and use of the word 'sly'); court rejected the recusal/bias claim.
Neither of those complaints has any merit.
11126: Availability of the statutory Orange Book delisting remedy under 21 U.S.C. § 355(c)(3)(D)(ii)(I) for an accused infringer, and the scope of the Hatch-Waxman listing rules and the 21 C.F.R. § 314.53 method-of-use regulation.
As the ’963 patent claims neither and has been asserted in a patent infringement action against Avadel, § 355(c)(3)(D)(ii)(I) provides Avadel with a delisting remedy.
11136: Taxable costs under 28 U.S.C. § 1920 for deposition transcript and related fees (realtime, rough transcripts, video, laptop and litigation package fees); whether these are taxable as printed or recorded transcripts.

We thus vacate and remand for the district court to consider whether these fees are the type that the Third Circuit would agree constitute fees for printed or electronically recorded transcripts or whether such convenience fees are beyond the scope of taxable costs.
11137: Taxability of trial exhibit copying, folders and labels as costs under 28 U.S.C. § 1920(4).
Trial exhibit copies and their associated folders and labels are taxable costs.
11138: Taxability of document production image conversion and export costs under 28 U.S.C. § 1920(4).

Because these costs are taxable under § 1920(4) and are reasonably supported by the Golden Declaration, we see no abuse of discretion in the district court's award of $31,358.78, which includes the "Production – Image Conversion and Export" costs.
11142: Whether the Board's termination decision on remand violated the court's mandate in Bennett II; held no violation of the mandate rule.
we conclude that the Board's termination decision did not violate our mandate in Bennett II.
11181: Compliance with the restoration order as to seniority and service credit at the Santa Maria office, reviewed for substantial evidence.
the agency proffers substantial evidence that neuters this issue.
11199: Motion to substitute under Fed. R. App. P. 43(b): the court held a party may not substitute for an original party that lacked standing to initiate the appeal, and denied the motion.
We hold that a party may not substitute under Rule 43(b) when the original party being substituted lacked standing to initiate the appeal.
11332: Whether the IPR petition adequately presented obviousness grounds for claims 6, 14, 22, 30 and 33 under 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(4), so the Board could decline to consider unargued claims; the court did not reach the merits of obviousness.
Keysight did no such elemental analysis, and indeed offered no argument, for claims 6, 14, 22, 30, and 33.
11344: Procedural issue under Rule 12(d): district court's reliance on extra-record academic texts and party-presentation challenge; court found the reliance improper but harmless because dismissal could be justified without extraneous matters.
The district court's reliance on extra-record academic texts — which were not presented by the parties — is incompatible with the procedural requirements of the Federal Rules.
11345: Make-whole remedy for reinstatement under the Whistleblower Protection Act: the Board failed to consider whether the employee would have applied for disability retirement absent the wrongful removal, so the remedy analysis was flawed and the decision was vacated.

Because the Board did not consider whether Mr. Arellanes would have formally applied for disability retirement in October 2014 even if he had not been removed on September 30, 2014, we vacate and remand to the Board.
11370: Lanham Act section 43(a) unfair competition claim: bad-faith (objectively baseless litigation) element; judgment of no liability vacated for new trial on bad-faith element.

Therefore, we reverse the district court's admissibility determination, vacate the judgment of no liability for unfair competition, and remand for a new trial on the bad faith element of Indect's Lanham Act claim.
11371: Scope of declaratory judgment of non-infringement extending to past, present and future customers (Kessler doctrine); vacated for lack of factual findings.
Because this extensive relief is not supported by sufficient findings, we vacate the district court's declaratory judgment and remand for further proceedings.
11391: Vacatur and remand to the Veterans Court to apply the amended 38 C.F.R. § 3.12 (character of discharge bar) after an intervening regulatory change; the court did not decide the merits, and did not reach the willful misconduct or harmless error arguments.
Because the Veterans Court did not have the benefit of the amended regulation, we vacate and remand.
11400: Step one of California anti-SLAPP analysis: whether the suit arises from protected activity (filing of patent applications) and whether the district court improperly collapsed step one into step two by assessing the merits of the trade secret claims; motion to strike denial vacated and remanded.

Thus, we vacate and remand for the district court to reconsider Tower's anti-SLAPP motion to strike by considering the possibility of trade secret misappropriation by Tower only at step two of its analysis.
11415: Trade secret misappropriation damages: whether the district court erred in precluding unjust enrichment damages under the DTSA and MUTSA and in limiting damages to a licensing-history royalty; the court held unjust enrichment recovery is available and vacated and remanded for a new trial on trade secret damages
We agree with Versata that it was entitled to pursue unjust enrichment damages; the district court legally erred when it precluded Versata from doing so.
11416: Trade secret damages: whether the district court properly reduced the jury's $22.386 million trade secret damages award to $0 on JMOL; the court partially vacated and remanded for a new trial on damages
Accordingly, we partially vacate the district court's JMOL zeroing out the jury's damages award and remand for a new trial on damages for trade secret misappropriation.
