11417: Breach of contract damages under Michigan law: whether the jury's $82.26 million award could be calculated with reasonable certainty; the court reinstated the jury award
We therefore conclude that the district court erred when it determined that Versata did not present any evidence that would allow the jury to calculate damages with reasonable certainty.
11418: Trade secret misappropriation liability: whether a plaintiff must show the defendant knew of the specific elements of a combination trade secret under the DTSA and MUTSA on Ford's cross-appeal from denial of JMOL; the court affirmed
Neither the DTSA nor the MUTSA, however, requires a plaintiff to show a defendant's knowledge of specific elements of combination trade secrets.
11432: Admissibility and reliability of technical expert testimony: whether an expert who acquired ordinary skill in the art after the invention date may offer infringement testimony from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill; court held no timing requirement exists
We agree with the district court that the proposed timing requirement is not a basis for excluding Dr. Kia's expert testimony as a matter of law.
11437: Sufficiency of notice of opposition pleadings (fair notice of claimed marks and priority basis), rejecting Chisena's pleading objection
Opposers' pleadings simply needed to afford Chisena fair notice of the claimed marks and the basis of its priority claims, and they did that.
11490: Remedy: vacatur of the CIT's universal permanent injunction and remand for the CIT to reconsider the scope of injunctive relief under the eBay factors and Trump v. CASA.

We vacate the CIT's grant of a permanent injunction universally enjoining the enforcement of the Trafficking and Reciprocal Tariffs and remand for the CIT to reevaluate the propriety of granting injunctive relief and the proper scope of such relief
11494: Rule 19(a)(1)(A) necessary-party question: whether the absent patent owner A&M is needed for complete relief given discovery needs; court held A&M is not a necessary party.
We hold A&M is not a necessary party and, thus, the district court erred in dismissing the suit under Rule 12(b)(7).
11507: Denial of a mandamus petition seeking to compel a VA Board decision and return of alleged illegal exactions: the court held no unreasonable delay under the TRAC factors and that an alternative remedy by appeal existed, so the writ was unavailable.
The Veterans Court, however, did not rely on an interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 19.2 in denying Mr. Prewitt's petition.
11508: Mandamus threshold: whether the petitioner showed no adequate alternative avenue of relief under Cheney, so the Veterans Court reasonably denied the mandamus petition seeking an earlier DIC effective date.
The Veterans Court therefore reasonably denied the petition for mandamus under Cheney.
11511: Mandamus standard for a veteran's petition: whether the veteran showed a clear and indisputable right to the writ and no other adequate means to obtain relief (Cheney requirements), so the Veterans Court properly denied the writ because an appeal of the RO decisions was an adequate alternative.
Because Mr. Bryan has an adequate alternative means to attain the relief he desires (i.e., appealing his RO decision(s)), the Veterans Court properly denied the writ.
11516: Statutory interpretation of 35 U.S.C. § 154(d) provisional rights: the court held provisional rights are granted only when a patent issues before its expiration date, which was the basis for dismissal.
we hold that provisional rights are granted only when a patent would issue with exclusionary rights (i.e., would issue before its expiration date).
11548: Nunc pro tunc substitution doctrine: whether the court may modify the Padgett v. Nicholson requirement that the veteran die after submission of the case for decision; the court held it is bound by Padgett and declined to expand the doctrine.
Padgett is a binding precedential opinion issued by a panel of this court and as such, "cannot be overruled or avoided unless or until the court sits en banc."
11559: Whether the agency materially breached the neutral employment reference provision of the settlement agreement (breach of settlement, substantial evidence review)
We find that substantial evidence supports the Board's decision that Ms. Long failed to prove the agency materially breached the neutral employment reference provision of the settlement agreement.
11569: Whether the Director's NHK-Fintiv institution instructions were substantive/legislative rules requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking under 5 U.S.C. § 553, or general statements of policy exempt under § 553(b); held general statements of policy, so no notice-and-comment was required.

We hold, in agreement with the district court, that the Director's instructions are a "general statement of policy" exempted from notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures by the express terms of § 553(b).
11591: Declining plaintiffs' renewed request to certify the scope-of-release question to the Indiana Supreme Court, because clear binding Indiana precedent (Newcastle and Rayl) already answers it.
For the reasons stated, we decline to certify the question of the scope of the Releases' conveyance to the Indiana Supreme Court.
11600: Whether Commerce's 15-day notice-of-intent deadline for domestic interested parties in sunset reviews is within its delegated rulemaking authority under the Tariff Act and does not conflict with 19 U.S.C. 1675(c)

We conclude that the Tariff Act provides Commerce 'fill up the details' authority is based on the statutory provision authorizing 'appropriate officers of the United States Government' to 'issue such regulations'
11669: Attorney-client privilege: the district court erred in holding that an attorney-client conflict of interest automatically terminated the representation and eliminated the privilege; the privilege is not vitiated by a conflict, and counsel may assert it on the client's behalf without first consulting the client.
The relevant cases hold that the attorney-client privilege is not vitiated because of the existence of an attorney-client conflict.
11701: CARES Act employee leave reimbursement claim rejected because the reimbursement authority covered only expenses through September 30, 2021, and the contract was awarded in 2022.
We agree with the Board that this statute permitted agencies to reimburse contractors only for expenses incurred through September 30, 2021.
11728: Invalidity of design patent for functionality (design dictated by utilitarian purpose); jury finding of non-functionality upheld on substantial evidence.
Substantial evidence supports the jury's verdict that the D877 Patent is not invalid for functionality.
11741: Statutory interpretation of the PSOB Act's 'substantial weight' and certified-facts provisions (34 U.S.C. § 10285(b)); court rejected petitioner's claim that the Director violated them because legal conclusions fall outside them and no identified finding of fact was ignored.
Insofar as those provisions concern findings of fact, we reject Mr. Lobo's assertion of error by the Director. Legal conclusions are outside the ambit of those provisions.
11757: Mandamus availability: whether adequate alternative remedy by appeal to the Veterans Court bars mandamus relief on the Board's merits errors.
Mr. Prewitt could challenge the merits of the Board's order through an appeal to the Veterans Court.
11779: Mandamus prerequisite: whether the petitioner had an adequate alternative remedy by appeal, which he did not invoke before the VA or the Board.
Vuksich's petition for mandamus was also properly denied because he had an adequate, alternative remedy available by appeal that was not invoked.
11803: Interpretation of the settlement agreement's confidentiality clause: whether intra-agency disclosure of the Last Chance Agreement to supervisors and the union representative breached the confidentiality term.
the most logical reading of the confidentiality provision is that it prohibits disclosure only to third parties—not that it prohibits disclosure to an agency's own supervisory employees.
11818: Timing of evidence in a false connection inquiry for a pending application: the court held §2(a) bars registration as of the time of examination, so post-filing evidence through the Board's reconsideration decision may be considered
For consistency, we hold § 2(a) bars registration of a pending application for a mark that falsely suggests a connection as of the time of examination.
11821: Lanham Act (non-patent) lost-profit damages in default context: denial of damages for other grand slam tournaments not specified in the complaint, held fundamentally unfair after default.
Accordingly, we are unpersuaded that the district court abused its discretion in its award of no non-patent damages.
11822: Post-judgment interest under 28 U.S.C. § 1961: district court erred in omitting statutorily mandated post-judgment interest.
The district court erred, however, in not awarding postjudgment interest, which is mandated by statute.
11854: Denial of mandamus petition under TRAC and Cheney for alleged unreasonable VA delay in processing a VR&E claim; court found no abuse of discretion and that adequate alternative means existed.
Mr. Windsor has not explained how or why this determination amounts to an abuse of discretion, and we conclude that it does not.
11929: Representative-claim designation in a §101 motion to dismiss: the district court erred in treating claim 1 as representative and finding ClickFunnels' representativeness argument frivolous, but the error was harmless because the court analyzed the dependent claims under step two anyway.
The district court's error, however, was harmless.
11943: Whether the agency's petition for review of the second initial decision required a certificate of compliance with an interim relief order under 5 C.F.R. 1201.116; court held none was required because the second decision contained no interim relief order.
Therefore, no certificate of compliance was required, and the MSPB did not err in denying Ms. Gharati's motion to dismiss.
11956: Whether the PTO may rely on the doctrine of foreign equivalents (translation of KAHWA as Arabic for coffee) given the undisputed well-established alternative English meaning of Kashmiri green tea; court held the doctrine does not apply as a matter of law.

Given the parties do not dispute KAHWA has a well-established alternative English meaning, as the Board decision admits, no translation is necessary since the doctrine of foreign equivalents does not apply as a matter of law.
11957: Trade-secret proper accessibility date: whether the secret became properly accessible when it could have been reverse-engineered (Feb. 2005) or when Intersil actually did so (Jan. 2006); court reversed the district court and set the earlier date.
We agree with Intersil and reverse the district court's finding of the proper accessibility date.
11958: Trade-secret head-start period: affirmed the district court's finding that the head-start period was 26 months.
We see no clear error in the district court's finding that the relevant duration was 26 months.
11959: Disgorgement amount: affirmed inclusion of all ISL29003 profits from iPod Touch sales traceable to the September 2006 design win and the attribution finding against Intersil's challenges.
We therefore affirm the inclusion in the disgorgement award of all profits attributable to Intersil's sales of ISL29003 units to Apple for use in the iPod Touch.
11960: TAOS cross-appeal seeking disgorgement of iPhone 3G profits: rejected because the design-win events occurred after the head-start end date.
We therefore reject the cross-appeal and affirm the disgorgement award made by the district court.
11963: Contract claim: rejected Intersil's double-recovery argument, holding the trade-secret and contract recoveries rested on non-overlapping sales.
It follows that there is no single injury and no double recovery, because the theories of liability arise from two separate and distinct injuries.
11964: Contract claim: rejected Intersil's argument that TAOS failed to prove the breach caused the damages (foreseeability under California law).
As TAOS would have reasonably expected to receive compensation for Intersil's use of its confidential information, we see no error in an award of reasonable-royalty damages.
11965: Contract claim: upheld reasonable-royalty award on Derivative Products that do not physically incorporate the trade secret, under the breach of confidentiality agreement.
On the evidence, the jury could reasonably include the Derivative Products in the group of sales made as a result of breach and thus award a royalty for those sales.
11966: Contract claim: upheld the jury's hypothetical-negotiation finding of a 10-year royalty term as supported by substantial evidence.
We conclude that the jury's royalty finding is supported by substantial evidence.
11968: Prejudgment interest: vacated and remanded the start date of interest accrual for sales made after the complaint was filed (Nov. 25, 2008 to June 3, 2014), under Texas and California law.
We vacate the district court's awards of prejudgment interest and remand the case to the district court for further consideration of this issue.
11988: Whether the district court improperly treated the Rule 12(c) motion as one for summary judgment by relying on supplemental briefing; the court held the claim language and attached patents were within the pleadings.
The Asserted Patents were attachments to the complaint. J.A. 25–222; J.A. 1333; J.A. 1337; J.A. 1340. Thus, the district court did not improperly look to information outside of the pleadings.
12007: Whether the Veterans Court engaged in impermissible fact-finding in characterizing the Board's reasons and the record, i.e., the scope of the Veterans Court's review and fact-finding limits. Court found no impermissible fact-finding.
We conclude that the Veterans Court's decision does not rely on impermissible fact-findings.
12033: Settlement enforcement: whether the agency breached the May 2015 settlement agreement by disclosing or failing to expunge disciplinary records from the official personnel file; the Board found compliance and the court affirmed that the record and substantial evidence support no breach.
the Board explicitly concluded that Ms. Martin failed to prove any breach of the settlement agreement.
12093: Conflict preemption of a Louisiana state-law conversion claim by federal patent law, as pled

Here, we agree with the district court that BearBox’s conversion claim is preempted because the conversion claim, as pled, is essentially an inventorship cause of action and patent infringement cause of action
12140: Mandamus standard: whether Robinson lacked an adequate alternative means to obtain relief, given a pending Veterans Court appeal challenging the same Board decision; court held the writ denial was not an abuse of discretion.

The Veterans Court's denial of the petition was not an abuse of discretion because Mr. Robinson had an adequate alternative means to attain the relief he requested—a pending appeal at the Veterans Court challenging the Board's February 27, 2023 decision.
12176: Scope of Board enforcement of a settlement agreement: the Board can enforce only the provisions contained in the settlement, and the petitioner did not assert breach of the 2018 Settlement's terms, so the petition to enforce was denied.
the Board can enforce only those contractual provisions that are contained in the parties’ settlement agreement.
12178: Effect of the broad release in the 2018 Settlement: the petitioner waived employment and disability-related claims, so no such relief could be granted even if argued.
Stephens waived any employment and disability related claims as part of the 2018 Settlement.
12180: Whether the district court abused its discretion in finding Insulet likely to succeed on its Defend Trade Secrets Act claim: it failed to address the statute of limitations, did not identify specific trade secrets with particularity, did not assess reverse engineering or patent disclosures, and did not assess independent economic value or knowing misappropriation. Trade secret/DTSA preliminary injunction issue, not covered by the patent codes.

In view of the failure to address the statute of limitations, the lack of a tailored analysis as to what specific information actually constituted a trade secret, as well as the finding that it was "hard to tell" what subset of that information was likely to have been misappropriated by EOFlow, we find that the district court abused its discretion in granting the October 24, 2023 preliminary injunction.
12181: Whether the district court properly found irreparable harm and weighed the public interest in granting the preliminary injunction; the court held irreparable harm was shown based on an error of law and unsupported speculation about a Medtronic acquisition, and gave only cursory public-interest analysis. Not covered by the patent codes.
But neither a generalized fear of a larger competitor nor any theoretical sale that can be remedied with damages constitutes a cognizable irreparable harm.
12186: Whether the Veterans Court applied the correct standard (TRAC) for mandamus relief on alleged unreasonable delay in adjudicating the Board appeal of the spinal claim; the court held the correct standard was applied and denied the writ
the Veterans Court applied the correct legal standard, i.e., the one set out in Telecommunications Research & Action Center v. FCC
12225: Validity and enforceability of the probationary-period waiver of Board appeal rights (contract ambiguity, lack of representation, consideration); court held the waiver unambiguous, knowing and voluntary, and supported by consideration. No existing code fits the contract-waiver question.
the contract is unambiguous because there is only one reasonable interpretation of the waiver provision.
12294: Walker Process fraud (attempted monopolization under Sherman Act §2) claim; district court granted summary judgment to Tenaris, which the Federal Circuit vacated because genuine disputes of material fact exist on the fraud element, anticompetitive conduct, relevant market and the measurement date.
Here, again, we conclude that genuine disputes of material fact preclude summary judgment. Thus, we vacate the trial court's judgment.
12306: Statutory interpretation of 15 U.S.C. § 9021 (PUA): whether the Secretary must pay PUA benefits directly to individuals absent a state agreement; court holds no direct payment obligation exists
We conclude the Secretary has no obligation to pay PUA benefits to individuals in the absence of an agreement with the state.
12477: Applicability of FAR 9.405-2 subcontract prohibitions to a debarred contractor: court held the provisions inapplicable because Monbo was not a subcontractor on the procurements.
These provisions are inapplicable because Ms. Monbo is not a subcontractor on the procurements in this appeal.
12526: Trade secret damages: whether the district court erred in precluding unjust enrichment damages under the DTSA and MUTSA; court held plaintiff may seek unjust enrichment damages and vacated the zeroing-out of the jury damages award, remanding for a new trial on damages.
We agree with Versata that it was entitled to pursue unjust enrichment damages; the district court legally erred when it precluded Versata from doing so.
12527: Breach of contract damages under Michigan law: whether the jury's $82,260,000 award was supported with reasonable certainty; court reinstated the jury award.
We agree and conclude that the district court erred when it reduced the jury award from $82,260,000 to $3.
12528: Trade secret misappropriation liability: whether plaintiff must show defendant knew of the specific elements of combination trade secrets; court held no such showing is required and affirmed denial of Ford's JMOL.
Neither the DTSA nor the MUTSA, however, requires a plaintiff to show a defendant's knowledge of specific elements of combination trade secrets.
12565: Validity of a settlement agreement resolving individual right of action (whistleblower reprisal) appeals: whether the settlement was involuntary, procured by attorney coercion or fraud, or entered without mental capacity, and whether the attorney-fee payment term was properly raised on petition for review.
On the record before us, we cannot say the Board's findings are unsupported by substantial evidence.
12594: Whether the IPR petition complied with 35 U.S.C. §312(a)(3) because the challenge to claim 17 of the '751 patent was allegedly incomprehensible; the court held the Board did not abuse its discretion in evaluating the petition.
The Board did not abuse its discretion by evaluating the petition on the merits or by failing to address Stryker’s critiques.
12610: Trade-secret misappropriation under DTSA and UUTSA: plaintiff failed to sufficiently identify and define its alleged trade secrets and show independent economic value, so summary judgment for defendants was affirmed.
We agree with the district court's conclusion that APT failed to sufficiently identify and define its alleged trade secrets under the statutory definition.
12626: Public Safety Officers' Benefits Act death benefit: whether the officer's death resulted from an 'injury' under 28 C.F.R. § 32.3 because the climatic conditions were not unusual, nonroutine, or unusually adverse; substantial evidence review of the Bureau's determination.
we affirm the Bureau's conclusion that Agent Afolayan did not sustain a compensable "injury" due to unusual, nonroutine, or unusually adverse climatic conditions
12627: Law of the case: whether petitioner may relitigate on remand the regulatory meaning of 'climatic conditions' (unusual or unusually adverse) already decided in Afolayan I.
law of the case prohibits Ms. Afolayan from reraising this issue.
12674: Whether a Lanham Act Section 43(a)(1)(B) false advertising counterclaim stated a cause of action where the accused falsely advertised a product as patented and the claim was linked to product nature, characteristics, or qualities; summary judgment for Crocs reversed (no fitting code; Dastar/Baden authorship bar held inapplicable).

We hold that a cause of action arises from Section 43(a)(1)(B) where a party falsely claims that it possesses a patent on a product feature and advertises that product feature in a manner that causes consumers to be misled about the nature, characteristics, or qualities of its product.
12709: Standard of review the Veterans Court applies to the Board's selection of an analogous diagnostic code under 38 C.F.R. § 4.20 for an unlisted condition: the court held selection is a fact-based application of law to facts, so the deferential 'arbitrary, capricious' standard of 38 U.S.C. § 7261(a)(3)(A) applies rather than de novo review.

Because selection of an analogous diagnostic code for rating unlisted conditions also concerns questions of fact, or at least questions of the application of law to the facts, the same deferential standard of review applies.
12757: Nexus between alleged infringement and irreparable harm for preliminary injunction, rejected as controlled by SB Opinion
we reject Celltrion's argument on the nexus issue, because Celltrion has presented no argument we have not already considered and rejected in the SB Opinion.
12906: Statutory interpretation of 35 U.S.C. §311(b): whether applicant admitted prior art can form the basis of an IPR ground when combined with prior art patents or printed publications (the Board's 'in combination' rule); court held the Board's interpretation contravened the plain meaning.

Under the plain meaning of § 311(b), the question is whether a petitioner has used AAPA as the basis, or part of the basis, of a ground—not whether the request relies on AAPA in combination with prior art patents or printed publications.
12907: Application of §311(b) to Ground 2: whether Apple's petitions expressly included applicant admitted prior art in the 'Basis' of Ground 2, violating §311(b); court held Apple was bound by its express phrasing and the Board erred in finding compliance.
we agree with Qualcomm that the Board misapplied § 311(b) to conclude that Ground 2 complies with the statute.
12919: Whether removal violated Ray's protected rights as a union president, i.e., whether the statements were protected union-representative activity or unprotected flagrant misconduct.
the arbitrator's finding that Mr. Ray was not acting in his Union president capacity, or alternatively that his statements were not protected by such capacity, is supported by substantial evidence.
12974: Alternative discretionary dismissal: the district court's decision to decline declaratory judgment jurisdiction even if jurisdiction existed, reviewed for abuse of discretion and affirmed.
we cannot say it abused its discretion in deciding that it would decline to exercise that jurisdiction.
13034: Party presentation principle: district court abused its discretion by invalidating asserted claims under §101 sua sponte on a ground no party raised; vacated and remanded for adjudication of issues the parties raised (§112 infringement and validity).

By rendering its decision on a ground not raised by any party at any stage of the proceedings, and by expressly declaring that it "sits not [as] an arbiter to resolve the disputes on the parties' favored terrain," the district court disregarded the longstanding principle of party presentation and, in doing so, abused its discretion.
13050: Whether the agency materially breached the confidentiality provision of the 2016 MSPB settlement agreement by cross-examining the appellant about her PIP and removal; no material breach found.
we see no reversible error in the Board's findings that the record of the Derr hearing—which was clearly before the Board (i.e., its AJ)—does not show a material breach by the agency.
13051: Whether the agency's cross-examination disclosures violated the Privacy Act routine-use promise incorporated into the settlement agreement; no violation found because the questions were a compatible use.
That reasonable characterization of Ms. Woodroof's testimony is ample ground for deeming the agency's questions on cross-examination a use compatible with the purpose of the record collection
13076: Whether the Board on remand complied with the appellate mandate (mandate rule scope) in revisiting the compressing limitation, which was not decided in the first appeal.
The Board did not err by revisiting the compressing limitation issue on remand.
13151: Berry's unsupported allegations of judicial bias, unethical conduct and conspiracy by the Board, Veterans Court and VA employees were rejected as lacking merit.
We thus conclude there is no merit to Mr. Berry's arguments on this issue.
13174: Scope of arbitrator's authority to impose random drug testing and medical-records release conditions as remedial terms not submitted to arbitration under the CBA.
We conclude the conditions imposed in the arbitrator's decision were within the scope of the arbitrator's authority under the collective bargaining agreement.
13244: Sufficiency of the trademark application's identification of goods and services (Trademark Rule 2.32(a)(6)); Board held the identification broad, vague and indefinite, so registration refusal was affirmed.
First, the Board found Mr. Duraisamy’s identification of goods and services unclear and indefinite.
13245: Requirement under 15 U.S.C. § 1112 to pay filing fees for each class of goods or services in a trademark application; applicant paid for only one class, and the requirement was upheld.
Second, the requirement for applicants to pay filing fees as part of their trademark applications is a statutory requirement.
13271: Whether HHS violated the Telework Enhancement Act by requiring Reed to sign a telework agreement and take leave until she did so; court held no violation because the continuity of operations plan superseded the voluntary telework policy.

This continuity of operations plan superseded HHS's previous telework policies and, in no uncertain terms, required all employees to enter telework agreements, in conformance with the requirements of the Act.
13273: Whether IPR petition relying on applicant-admitted prior art (AAPA) as general background knowledge violated 35 U.S.C. 311(b); court held it did not
The IPR petition did not violate § 311(b).
13293: Illinois absolute litigation privilege bars Atturo's tortious interference (prospective business expectancy), unfair competition and unjust enrichment counterclaims (state-law privilege); judgment for Atturo reversed.
we reverse the district court's judgment as to Atturo's counterclaims for tortious interference, unfair competition, and unjust enrichment.
13294: Illinois absolute litigation privilege bars Atturo's defamation and Illinois Deceptive Trade Practices Act counterclaims; judgment for Toyo affirmed.
Accordingly, we agree with the district court that Illinois's absolute litigation privilege bars Atturo's defamation and IDTPA counterclaims.
13309: AIA derivation proceeding: whether the petitioner established derivation (conception and communication) and the respondent's independent-conception defense; Board found Selner proved earlier independent conception, so derivation claim failed.
we affirm the Board's judgment for Selner.
13310: Board's evidentiary rule-of-reason corroboration of inventor testimony in derivation proceeding (emails, metadata, corroboration requirement).
The Board did not err in its application of the law and did not abuse its discretion in its evidentiary rulings.
13311: Whether actual reduction to practice is required for complete conception in derivation.
Actual reduction to practice was not required for complete conception of the Invention.
13335: Antitrust unlawful tying liability under Sherman Act: whether substantial evidence supported the jury's finding that Ingevity's honeycombs were staple goods, so the statutory patent misuse defense under 35 U.S.C. 271(d) failed

In sum, because the jury's verdict rested on permissible inferences and credibility determinations supported by the record, substantial evidence supports the finding that Ingevity's honeycombs are staple goods.
13337: Antitrust damages: whether BASF had to disaggregate lawful patent enforcement damages and whether the damages were speculative (material cause standard)
BASF needed to show that Ingevity's conduct was a material or substantial cause of its injury.
13384: Affirmance of Board dismissal under 38 U.S.C. § 7105(d) for failure to identify a determination on appeal, on the ground that the claimant may pursue the asserted unadjudicated claim before the regional office; the court did not decide the interpretation of § 7105 or the validity of 38 C.F.R. § 20.904(b).
In reliance on the availability of that procedure, we therefore affirm the Veterans Court's affirmance of the Board's dismissal.
13390: Motion to strike portions of petitioner's reply brief and supplemental expert declaration; Board's reliance on challenged materials without ruling on the motion
BJES does not explain what, if any, new arguments those specific portions raise such that it was improper for the Board to rely on them
13414: Whether the Postal Service breached the settlement agreement by contacting OWCP about the employee's excluded workers' compensation claim (settlement enforcement / contract interpretation; no existing code fits).
The Postal Service did not breach the settlement agreement.
13415: Whether an alleged pre-settlement oral promise that the $10,000 payment would be tax-free was enforceable despite the integration clause and the tax-liability provision (settlement enforcement / contract interpretation; no existing code fits).
We cannot rewrite the agreement to include provisions not set forth in the written instrument.
13429: Reviewability under the APA: court rejected the government's argument that the List 3 and 4A tariffs were non-reviewable presidential action because they were agency action under delegated authority.

We affirm the trial court's well-reasoned conclusion that actions involving discretionary authority delegated by Congress to the President are distinct from those involving authority delegated by Congress to an agency, and that the List 3 and 4A tariffs implicate the latter category of actions reviewable under the APA.
13430: Applicant entity designation: whether the owner name and stated legal entity type were inconsistent and required clarification before registration (application formality under 37 C.F.R. 2.32).
First, the Board properly determined an inconsistency between the owner name and entity type.
13431: Description of the mark: whether the applicant's description of a non-color-claimed stylized mark, including color references and a registered mark name, was acceptable under 37 C.F.R. 2.37 and 2.52(b)(1).
Second, the Board properly determined that Mr. Duraisamy failed to submit an acceptable description of the mark.
13432: Identification of goods and services: whether amendments were indefinite and impermissibly broadened the original identification in Class 42 and added goods in other classes under 37 C.F.R. 2.71(a).

Third, the Board properly determined that Mr. Duraisamy's identification of goods and/or services is indefinite and his amendments to the identification section exceeded the scope of his original application.
13442: Statutory interpretation of the Continued Dumping and Subsidy Offset Act (19 U.S.C. § 1675c): whether CDSOA requires Customs to distribute delinquency interest under 19 U.S.C. § 1505(d) to affected domestic producers; held it unambiguously does not.
In sum, the CDSOA unambiguously excludes delinquency interest from distribution to affected producers.
13447: Admissibility of infringement expert testimony under Daubert (weight versus admissibility; testing not required); excluded testimony reinstated
Thus, we conclude that the district court abused its discretion by excluding the testimony of ParkerVision's infringement experts.
13449: Whether invalidity of VA regulations conflicting with the statutes could support relief; court held claimant lacked injury so no relief warranted, declining to reach the regulatory challenge merits and the jurisdiction question.
Mr. Loomis is ineligible for benefits by statute, and so any irregularity in the regulations causes him no injury and warrants no relief.
13509: Lanham Act trademark infringement of THE COMFY registrations (likelihood of confusion under Sleekcraft factors, including source-identifier use and de minimis actual confusion). The court held substantial evidence did not support the jury verdict and reversed denial of JMOL. No P or T code fits this trademark issue in a patent case.

we conclude that, based on the undisputed evidence viewed in the light most favorable to Cozy Comfort, no reasonable jury could have found that Cozy Comfort met its burden to prove trademark infringement.
13534: Dismissal of complaint under Rule 12(b)(5) for insufficient service of process; no good cause or excusable neglect for improper personal service by plaintiff
We see no abuse of discretion in the district court's determination that neither good cause nor excusable neglect applies to Mr. Behnamian's failure to effect proper service of process.
13540: Frivolousness of the appeal and the Court of Federal Claims' 28 U.S.C. §1915(a)(3) certification that an appeal would not be taken in good faith; motion to proceed in forma pauperis on appeal denied and appeal dismissed.
We deny his motion to proceed in forma pauperis, and we dismiss his appeal.
13546: Literal falsity element of a Lanham Act false advertising claim (15 U.S.C. 1125(a)(1)(B)) for the CRTN-3 'increase vasodilation' label; judgment reversed because no reasonable jury could find literal falsity. Outside the enumerated trademark codes, which address registration and cancellation.
Because no reasonable jury could find CRTN-3’s statement of “increase vasodilation” is literally false, BPI’s Lanham Act claim for false advertising necessarily fails.
13606: Whether K2 was a necessary or indispensable party under RCFC 19 (joinder); held not necessary because K2 forwent intervention, reputational interest insufficient, and injunction binds only USPS.
we conclude that K2 was not a necessary or indispensable party under either standard.
13656: Whether the Veterans Court properly applied Tadlock v. McDonough and Hart v. Mansfield to find a harmless, nonprejudicial error and that service records were not needed to assess current disability; court found no error.
We discern no error in the Veterans Court applying the teachings of those cases to Mr. Rodriguez's appeal. We therefore affirm on this issue.
13666: Harmless error: assuming without deciding that the Veterans Court erred on jurisdiction over a request for a Board referral directive under 38 C.F.R. § 20.904(b), Stiles showed no prejudice, so the dismissal is affirmed.

Mr. Stiles has identified no prejudice, i.e., no harmful error, even if we assume that the Veterans Court was wrong about its jurisdiction to consider directing the Board to refer the at-issue claims to the regional office.
13676: Whether the Veterans Court erred in interpreting its own prior decision (Hooper 2021) and denying a motion to recall the mandate, i.e., whether that decision determined the finality of a 2008 rating decision; court held no error in the Veterans Court's reading of its prior remand decision.
Mr. Hooper has not persuaded us that the Veterans Court committed any error in interpreting its Hooper 2021 decision.
13705: Grant of judgment as a matter of law for DePuy on infringement and damages, predicated on the exclusion of the expert testimony; reversed as following from the exclusion rulings, with the court not deciding sufficiency of non-expert evidence.
We also reverse the district court's grant of JMOL, which was predicated on the lack of evidence remaining in the record after the court excluded Dr. Yassir's and Dr. Neal's opinions.
13730: Whether the construction of 'stoichiometric quantities' term is reviewable; court declined to review because the stipulated judgment did not implicate the term
we decline to review the district court's construction of this term.
13776: Whether the Board should have vacated the reexamination request for lack of a substantial new question of patentability; court held the request clearly raised an SNQ.
the request for ex parte reexamination clearly raised a substantial new question of patentability.
13795: Whether a Board-approved settlement agreement in a 2016 IRA appeal could be rescinded for the agency's alleged breach (nonpayment), or whether the claim belonged in a petition for enforcement; court held rescission unavailable on this record and affirmed.

we see no error in the Board's conclusion that the proper procedure for making such an argument is one Ms. Payton has not invoked, S. Appx. 1 n.2: a petition for enforcement of the settlement agreement under 5 C.F.R. § 1201.182.
13817: Whether the VA's Final Rule applying the lesser-of/Medicare fee schedule payment methodology to all noncontract ambulance transports exceeds the statutory authority granted by 38 U.S.C. § 111(b)(3)(C), which is limited to transports to or from a Department facility; held the rule exceeds that authority and is not in accordance with law under the APA.
Because the Final Rule exceeds the statutory authority vested in the VA by § 111(b)(3)(C), we grant the petition and set aside the Final Rule.
13827: Section 1498 government-use immunity defense (authorization and consent, 'for the Government' use, including Terry demonstrations and the 15 U.S.C. 638 SBIR Phase III argument); summary judgment for AeroVironment affirmed.

At bottom, there is simply not sufficient evidence from which a reasonable jury could find that AeroVironment engaged in infringing conduct that was not for the benefit of, and with authorization of and consent from, the government.
13903: Contract interpretation under California law: whether the 2012 Agreement's disputed statement incorporates the entire Contract of Sale (indemnification limitation) or only portions; court held the agreement unambiguous and incorporated in its entirety, so Samsung's indemnification clause applies. Coded as X99 because contract interpretation between private parties in a third-party contract dispute is not an enumerated code for this case type.
Accordingly, we conclude that the 2012 Agreement unambiguously incorporates the Contract of Sale in its entirety.
13941: Whether the Veterans Court erred in denying a request for appointment of counsel, holding that the court lacks authority to appoint counsel under its precedent and that no statutory, regulatory, or constitutional authority requires it.
We therefore reject Mr. Nyepah's contention that the Veterans Court erred by not appointing counsel for him.
13957: Whether to certify a question of Florida law to the Florida Supreme Court; court declined certification as unwarranted.
13994: Whether the CRU abused its discretion in applying 37 C.F.R. § 41.50(b) by refusing to reopen prosecution and referring the response to the Board as a request for rehearing.
we hold the CRU did not abuse its discretion in rejecting the request to reopen prosecution and referring the request to the Board as a request for rehearing under 37 C.F.R. § 41.50(b)(2).
13997: Whether the Bates '591 application claims, amended after the critical date, are time-barred under 35 U.S.C. § 135(b)(1), which turns on whether pre-critical-date claims support them under a two-way versus one-way materiality test. The court held the Board applied the wrong test and that the claims are materially different, so they are time-barred.

On this record, we conclude that as a matter of law the pre-critical date claims are materially different from the post-critical date claims. The '591 application is time-barred under section 135(b)(1).
14005: Unpaid overtime claim dismissed because the plaintiff was an FLSA-exempt employee and so could not state a viable claim; affirmed on an alternative ground supported by the record
Mr. Strong therefore could not have stated a viable claim for unpaid overtime, and we affirm the trial court's dismissal of this portion of Mr. Strong's complaint.
14047: Trade secret misappropriation (RIUTSA): whether the alleged signal acquisition trade secret was adequately identified, so that the district court properly removed it from jury consideration; no code covers trade secret existence or scope
we are not persuaded that the district court erred by excluding the alleged signal acquisition trade secret from jury consideration.
14089: Existence of a valid contract for breach of contract claim: whether HeS established a contract formed with a government official having actual authority to bind the government under the EULA. The court held no valid contract was shown.
Thus, HeS fails to establish the first element of the breach of contract allegation: the existence of a valid contract.
14091: Copyright registration validity under 17 U.S.C. § 411(b): whether HeS's registrations were invalid because deposit copies contained knowingly inaccurate information that would have caused the Register to refuse registration. The court held the registrations invalid, barring the infringement claim.

Because HeS submitted deposit copies with known inaccurate information, and the Copyright Office confirmed it would have refused registration had it known of these inaccuracies, HeS’s copyright registrations are invalid.
14126: Whether the removal was retaliation for union activity in violation of 5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(9)(A); Board finding that union activity played no role affirmed.

The AJ credited testimony that demonstrated Ms. Wilson's removal was "wholly unrelated to any union activity" but instead due to Ms. Wilson "ha[ving] accessed sensitive . . . information within the eOPF system on multiple occasions."
14132: Board authority to supplement or substitute its own factual findings for those of the administrative judge without overturning demeanor-based credibility findings; Board acted within its authority under 5 C.F.R. § 1201.117(b)
Here, the Board did not overturn any credibility findings by the AJ.
14162: Recognition of the 2021 Afghan Land Court judgment under Restatement (Fourth) of Foreign Relations Law section 484; Board erred in declining recognition at summary judgment, without deciding recognition.
We do not decide that the 2021 Decision was entitled to recognition as a foreign judgment.
14163: Act of state doctrine as a bar to the Lessors' contract relief; court held the doctrine does not bar the requested relief.
We conclude that the act of state doctrine does not bar the Lessors' request for relief.
14193: Injunction against Commerce's 154.33% cash-deposit rate under the eBay/preliminary-injunction standards (irreparable harm, balance of hardships, public interest); injunction affirmed.
we hold that the Trade Court correctly ruled that the 154.33% rate could not stand, and it was therefore in the public interest to enjoin enforcement of that rate
14197: Board invalidated claims 11 and 12 on a ground Samsung never raised in its petition; the Board may not invalidate on grounds it identifies sua sponte, so the finding was vacated.
Thus, we vacate the Board's invalidity finding as to claims 11 and 12.
14204: Interpretation of a 2023 MSPB settlement agreement: whether the agreement unambiguously required payment to the employee rather than his non-attorney representative, so the VA did not breach. Not a listed merits code; no federal-employment code fits settlement-enforcement contract interpretation.
These provisions unambiguously specify that the VA must pay Mr. Lynn the settlement payment.
14205: Whether the VA breached the implied duty of good faith and fair dealing in performing the settlement agreement, which the court held cannot be violated by compliance with unambiguous terms.
because the VA's compliance with the unambiguous terms of the Agreement cannot violate that duty.
14211: Scope of judicial review: court declined to review the merits de novo because the Board lacked a quorum and no Board review of the initial decision occurred, so the 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c) standard applies.
There is no basis in the absence of a quorum for this court to conduct de novo review.
14212: Whether the Veterans Court properly denied Taylor's petition for a writ of mandamus because he failed to show a clear legal right to relief, no adequate alternative channel, and appropriateness; the court affirmed the denial.
Accordingly, we affirm the Veterans Court's holding that Mr. Taylor failed to establish entitlement to a writ of mandamus.
14215: Veterans Court's denial of Taylor's motion for panel review under Rule 35 as premature because the petition had not yet been decided; the court found this correct.
The Veterans Court correctly denied the motion as premature because Rule 35 is a post-decision review, and the Veterans Court had not yet issued a decision on the petition.
14266: Alternative holding on the merits: even if raised timely, the settlement agreement's validity was not overcome because the petitioner bore a heavy burden and offered only conclusory allegations of coercion and fraud, with counsel representing her throughout.
A bare allegation of coercion is not sufficient to set aside the parties' settlement agreement.
14272: Whether future lost earnings are recoverable as compensatory damages under the WPA corrective action provision, 5 U.S.C. § 1221(g)(1)(A)(ii); no existing code fits this remedy question.
We find that future lost earnings are recoverable as compensatory damages pursuant to § 1221(g)(1)(A)(ii).
14273: Burden of proof for WPA pecuniary compensatory damages; the Board erred by requiring the employee to guarantee future employment rather than applying the preponderance standard; no existing code fits.
We find the Board erred by improperly raising the burden for Perlick to establish these damages.
14369: FTCA money damages claim against USPTO dismissed for failure to present an administrative claim under 28 U.S.C. § 2675(a) (exhaustion)
We therefore affirm the district court's dismissal of her claim for money damages.
14371: APA claim on the '395 application abandonment dismissed for failure to exhaust administrative remedies (no petition to revive)
Because Ms. Winfrey failed to exhaust her administrative remedies, we affirm the district court's dismissal of her APA claim relating to the '395 patent application.
14374: Whether the PTO waived, or is judicially or equitably estopped from asserting, a descriptiveness refusal based on its withdrawal of a similar refusal in a separate application proceeding (FORMULARYHUB.com); court held none applied.
Accordingly, the Board correctly concluded that equitable estoppel does not apply.
14378: Statutory construction of 35 U.S.C. § 156(c) under Hatch-Waxman Act: whether PTE for a reissued patent is calculated from the original patent's issue date; the court held 'the patent' refers to the original patent, affirming PTE of five years (Merck wins)
We hold that, in the context of reissued patents, the reference to “the patent” in subsection 156(c) is to the original patent.
14405: Pre-initiation industry support determination under 19 U.S.C. 1673a(c)(1)(A)(ii) and (c)(4): Commerce's industry support calculation was supported by substantial evidence, including the double-counting question; the duty to examine accuracy of petition evidence does not extend to the industry support determination.
Because substantial evidence supports Commerce's determination that it was, we affirm.
14496: Ohio Uniform Trade Secrets Act: sufficiency of trade secret definiteness and public disclosure/secrecy for TS 24, affirming JMOL that TS 24 is not a trade secret
We find no reversible error in the district court's determination that TS 24 is not entitled to trade secret status.
14497: Ohio Uniform Trade Secrets Act: definiteness and use elements for TS 7, TS 11 and TS 20, affirming JMOL for Goodyear
We find no reversible error in the district court's determination that these trade secrets are not sufficiently definite and were not used by Goodyear.
14498: Ohio Uniform Trade Secrets Act: insufficient evidence of Goodyear's use of TS 23, affirming JMOL for Goodyear
Coda presents insufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to find that Goodyear used TS 23.
14525: Orange Book listing and delisting eligibility under 21 U.S.C. 355(b)(1)(A)(viii) and 355(j)(5)(C): whether a patent that claims only device components of a drug-device combination product 'claims the drug' and must be listed, which requires claiming at least the active ingredient.

To list a patent in the Orange Book, that patent must, among other things, claim the drug for which the applicant submitted the application and for which the application was approved. And to claim that drug, the patent must claim at least the active ingredient.
14586: Lanham Act false advertising claim (15 U.S.C. 1125(a)(1)(B)): statements about Mighty Line tape were not literally false puffery; summary judgment for defendants affirmed.
The district court did not err in granting summary judgment on Spota's false advertising claim.
14588: Denial of plaintiffs' motion to recuse or disqualify the district judge under Liteky and the Sixth Circuit standard; no abuse of discretion.
Accordingly, there was no abuse of discretion in the district court's denial of the plaintiffs' recusal motion.
14644: Denial of motions for recusal of two panel judges based on their prior participation in related cases.
Judicial recusal is therefore not required simply because members of the panel in this case have participated in other cases raising similar issues.
14650: Reassignment of the case to a different district court judge on remand, based on the trial judge's statements and the appearance of fairness.
For these reasons, we remand the case for trial before a different district court judge.
14653: Whether the Veterans Court's harmless-error determination on the Board's treatment of illustrative TDIU jobs rested on a legal error: the Veterans Court overread Smith v. Shinseki and applied a rigid harmlessness rule. The court vacated and remanded for the Veterans Court to revisit the challenge.
We conclude that the Veterans Court may have relied on legal error in its determination of harmless error.
14696: Vacatur of a preliminary injunction on a trademark infringement claim because the likelihood-of-success finding rested on the erroneous rejection of the unlawful use defense; the court also said the other preliminary injunction factors may have been tainted and need reconsideration.
We thus vacate the district court's grant of VPR's motion for a preliminary injunction and remand the case to the court for further proceedings consistent with this decision.
14707: Whether a non-attorney executor may represent an estate (an entity) pro se in the Court of Federal Claims under Rule 83.1(a)(4); held he could not.
As the court observed, Rule 83.1 precludes non-attorneys from representing an entity before the court.
14789: Trade-secret protectability under California UTSA: the four asserted trade secrets (internal pockets, mesh tabs, absorbable sutures, instrument list) were not protectable because generally known or not kept secret; JMOL reversed on trade-secret misappropriation.

We hold that there was no legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that plaintiffs had met their burden to show that each of the asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law and reverse the district court's denial of JMOL on the trade-secret claims.
14790: Breach of the non-disclosure agreement: no Confidential Information beyond the asserted trade secrets, so no sufficient evidence of breach; JMOL reversed on breach-of-contract claim.

Because we hold that the undisputed evidence showed each alleged trade secret did not qualify as a trade secret under California law, we also hold that there was not sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to find liability for breach of contract.
14791: Trade-secret remedies: vacatur of willful and malicious misappropriation finding, reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and permanent injunction in light of no trade secrets being misappropriated.

In light of our holding that no trade secrets were misappropriated, we vacate the district court's finding of willful and malicious misappropriation, the reasonable royalty award, the exemplary damages award, and the permanent injunction.
14792: Counterfeiting under 15 U.S.C. 1117: sufficient evidence supported liability for use of the Penuma mark in connection with goods; denial of JMOL affirmed and jury instruction upheld.
We thus affirm the district court's denial of JMOL on counterfeiting.
14812: Lanham Act section 43(a)(1)(B) false advertising: summary judgment for defendant affirmed because no evidence of injury proximately caused by the Design Manual misrepresentations (causation and presumption of injury).

In sum, no reasonable jury could conclude that SME Steel has demonstrated injury in this case, and the district court did not err in granting summary judgment in Seismic Bracing's favor on false advertising.
14813: Lanham Act section 43(a)(1)(A) false association (corporate persona): summary judgment for defendant affirmed because no reasonable jury could find a likelihood of confusion; statutory standing not reached.

Given the admitted care that customers will exercise in reviewing materials related to the bids and selecting BRBs, as well as the absence of evidence of actual confusion, we agree that no reasonable jury could conclude that there was a likelihood of confusion.
14814: Copyright infringement damages: summary judgment affirmed because the copyright holder's indirect-profits claim lacked evidence of a nexus between the infringement and Seismic Bracing's profits.
SME Steel's copyright damages contention, on which SME Steel bears the ultimate burden, was based only on speculation, which is insufficient.
14818: Whether the APJ violated executive-branch ethics regulations (5 C.F.R. 2635.402, 2640.202, 2635.501, 2635.502) by failing to recuse for his de minimis Cisco stock holding; court held no violation.
Because APJ McNamara at all times complied with those regulations, he did not violate the executive branch ethics rules.
14830: Validity of the en banc proceeding under 28 U.S.C. section 46(c) and the Judicial Conduct and Disability Act; EcoFactor argued the en banc court was statutorily improper and could not alter the panel decision, and the court rejected that challenge.

Because the en banc panel consists of fewer than all judges in regular active service, as required by 28 U.S.C. § 46(c), EcoFactor argues this en banc court is statutorily improper and cannot alter the decision of the three-judge panel. We do not agree.
14841: Refusal to consider extra-record evidence submitted for the first time on appeal; the court held it is not part of the record and that 5 C.F.R. § 1201.115(d) does not apply to the Federal Circuit.

Because we are limited to reviewing decisions of the Board based on the record before the deciding official, we decline to base our judgment on evidence that was not part of the record before the administrative judge.
14842: Dismissal of a pro se IFP complaint against the USPTO as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i), as duplicative and lacking an arguable basis in law or fact

Based on the totality of the circumstances, we conclude that the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing Mr. Perry's complaint as frivolous because his claims lack an arguable basis in law or fact.
14843: Whether the district judge erred by not recusing herself under 28 U.S.C. § 455; reviewed for plain error because recusal was never moved for below
We thus find no error in the district court judge's decision not to recuse herself.
14846: Board's finding that Lucas was not eligible for waiver of the overpayment debt, held to be within the Board's limited jurisdiction.
the Board did not err—it acted within its jurisdiction in finding that Ms. Lucas was not eligible for waiver of her debt
14855: Law-of-the-case doctrine: whether the administrative judge was bound by the Board's 2011 nonfrivolous-allegation holding; court held the doctrine applies only to issues actually decided and rejected the argument.
The law-of-the-case doctrine only applies to issues that "have actually been decided."
14867: Whether the PTO had statutory authority under 35 U.S.C. § 316(a)(4) to promulgate the estoppel regulation § 42.73(d)(3)(i), which appellant argued was substantive rather than procedural.

We reject SoftView's argument and hold that section 42.73(d)(3) of the PTO's regulations was lawfully promulgated pursuant to the agency's rulemaking authority under section 316(a)(4) of the Patent Act.
14913: Whether the Veterans Court properly denied a mandamus petition alleging unreasonable VA delay in adjudicating claims, applying the TRAC factors
We affirm the Veterans Court's denial of mandamus, and we dismiss the appeal as to other issues.
14929: Injunction barring the Army from proceeding with the award to F3EA; vacated because the findings supporting it were vacated
Hence, we vacate the order enjoining the Army from proceeding with its award to F3EA.
14973: Legal standard for constructive possession of documents for the administrative record before the Veterans Court (relevance and reasonableness under Euzebio II); court found no legal error in the standard applied.
We see no legal error with the standard applied by the Veterans Court.
14977: Whether Commerce abused its discretion in rejecting as untimely Tau-Ken's questionnaire response filed 1 hour and 41 minutes after the extended deadline, under its own deadlines and the Grobest considerations; the court found an abuse of discretion and did not reach facts otherwise available or adverse inference.
Commerce made a clear error of judgment and thus abused its discretion in rejecting Tau-Ken’s September 16 submission.
14988: Legality of $10,000 incentive awards to class representatives under Trustees v. Greenough and Central Railroad v. Pettus; the court held incentive awards are not per se barred and upheld the awards as reasonable.
we join the vast majority of our sister circuits in holding that incentive awards are permitted so long as they are found to be reasonable by a district court.
14992: Public access to CIT judicial records and confidentiality designations: whether 19 U.S.C. 1516a abrogates the common law right of access, and whether the Commission may automatically designate all questionnaire responses as confidential; court held no abrogation, the practice is unlawful, and the CIT's remand order was proper.
We conclude that section 1516a preserves the common law right of access.
15002: Judicial estoppel bars Belanger from arguing that the basis of the jury's damages award cannot be determined, so the court can identify the convoyed-sales amount.
Belanger is judicially estopped from contending otherwise
15012: Substantial-evidence review of the BJA's PSOB Act determination that the firefighter's stroke death was not in the line of duty (whether the CFD had an official mandatory training or fitness program under 28 C.F.R. § 32.13 and 34 U.S.C. § 10281(k)).
We conclude that substantial evidence supports the BJA's determination that Mr. Weston did not die "in the line of duty."
15035: Statutory authority of VA to promulgate the Background Check Provision (38 C.F.R. 1.601(a)(2)) under 38 U.S.C. 501 and 5722-5723; court held authority exists.
The Background Check Provision is within the VA's statutory authority to promulgate regulations regarding information security.
15038: Statutory authority of VA to promulgate the Inspection Provision (38 C.F.R. 1.602(c)(1)); court held the provision exceeds VA's statutory authority and set it aside.
MVA argues the Inspection Provision exceeds the VA's statutory authority. We agree.
15084: Whether the Veterans Court abused its discretion or committed legal error in denying a mandamus petition, holding that the normal appeal process was an adequate alternative means to relief despite repeated Board remands (adequate alternative means standard for mandamus).
We see no error or abuse in this analysis. The Veterans Court used the correct legal precedent.
15135: Mandamus: whether the Veterans Court legally erred by considering postpetition events (mootness) in evaluating a mandamus petition; no legal error found
We therefore see no legal error in the Veterans Court's consideration of events that occurred after Mr. Windsor filed his mandamus petition.
15136: Mandamus: whether the adequate-alternative-means requirement defeated the writ to compel scheduling and adjudication of the section 1151 claim; the court held the writ unavailable because other adequate means existed

This demonstrates that Mr. Windsor did not satisfy the legal standard for issuance of the writ, which requires that the party seeking issuance of the writ have no other adequate means to attain the relief he desires.
15139: Mandamus: whether the Veterans Court should have compelled expedited adjudication of the section 1151 claim under TRAC; no undue delay found

We read the Veterans Court's decision as also holding that there has been no undue delay in the processing of Mr. Windsor's claim to warrant expeditious adjudication of his claim, and we see no error in that conclusion.
15194: Denial of the 28 U.S.C. §455 recusal and vacatur motion as to the Ajax ground, decided on harmless-error grounds under Liljeberg without reaching the merits.
We therefore affirm the district court's denial of the motion to recuse on the Ajax ground without reaching the merits.
15217: Application of the doctrine of foreign equivalents (threshold translation of French word VETEMENTS into English; ordinary American purchaser stop-and-translate analysis) as a threshold step for the registrability determination
We hold that unless it is unlikely that the ordinary American purchaser would stop and translate the word into its English equivalent, the doctrine of foreign equivalents applies.
15250: Summary judgment for Galderma on state-law breach of contract and trade-secret misappropriation claims because Truinject has no viable damages; the court did not reach other grounds.
With damages off the table, no relief can be given to Truinject for breach of contract; and we need not address other grounds for rejecting the breach-of-contract claim.
